questions.q: Teena orders a lamp listed at Rs 900 on a shopping app. The seller is in another city, she pays online and the lamp is delivered. Her classmate says, 'This is not a market, because Teena never met the seller.' Which reply is correct?
o: It is a market: both sides agreed a price, and markets can be online
It is not a market: a market must have a building where goods are kept
It is a market only because the goods were delivered to her doorstep
It is not a market: only a bazaar or haat can be called a market place
questions.a: The chapter says a market can be at a physical place or online, and every market has a buyer, a seller and an agreed price. The lamp sale has all three. Delivery is not what makes it a market, and a building is not required.

questions.q: A family spends Rs 9,000 in a month: Rs 3,500 on food, Rs 1,500 on clothes for the children, Rs 2,000 on rent for their home, Rs 500 on a streaming subscription and Rs 1,500 on upgrading to a newer phone. Taking food, clothing and shelter as needs, as the chapter does, the money spent on wants is Rs ___.
Anil says, 'Whatever I spend on every single day is a need.' Which item from his daily spending shows that he is wrong, going by the chapter's definition of a need?
o: Rs 40 on a cold drink each evening that he buys daily but could do without
Rs 15 on drinking water that the family uses on each day of the week
Rs 10 on a packet of milk for the family's morning tea each day
Rs 60 on the lunch that he eats at school each day of the week
questions.a: A need is something a person requires to survive, such as food, water, clothing and shelter. The cold drink is bought daily but is desired and not essential, so it is a want; buying something often does not make it a need. Drinking water, milk and lunch (food) are needs.

questions.q:
A guava seller asks Rs 80 per kg. A buyer offers Rs 30. After some bargaining they settle at Rs 45 per kg and the buyer takes 2 kg.
1. Rs 45 per kg is the price in this transaction, because it is the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller is willing to sell.
2. Rs 80 per kg is the price, because the seller named it first and the buyer must accept it.
3. If the two had not reached an amount both accepted, the transaction might not have taken place.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 follow the chapter: price is the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller willing to sell, and without such a point the transaction may not take place. Statement 2 is false: a seller's first ask is not the price; buyer and seller negotiate until a mutually agreeable price is reached.

questions.q:
The history club of a Bengaluru school puts up this extract at its exhibition. Fernao Nuniz wrote: 'There were craftsmen, also, working in their streets, so that you saw made there golden jewels and gewgaws... sellers of cloths... it is a mystery how there should be an abundance of everything therein.' Domingos Paes listed grains, seeds, milk, oil, silk, cows, horses, quails and partridges.
(a) Sort these four goods into needs and wants, using the chapter's definitions: grains, milk, golden jewels, rubies.
(b) The chapter says markets do two things: they make goods and services available to people, and they connect people, traditions and ideas. Which of the two does this extract show better, and why does it show the other one less?
(c) The extract speaks of sellers and goods but never mentions a price. Which feature of a market is therefore not visible in it, and why must it have existed for any sale in the bazaar to happen?
(d) The club must choose one caption for the entrance: (i) 'Hampi: where every kind of good, from grain to rubies, could be had in one place' or (ii) 'Hampi: where craftsmen made in their streets what they sold'. Choose one and justify it using the extract.
questions.a: (a) Grains and milk are needs (required to survive); golden jewels and rubies are wants (desired but not essential for survival). (b) The first: the long lists of grain, oil, silk, cloth and jewels show goods being made available to the people of the city. The extract tells us nothing about people, traditions or ideas meeting, so that second role cannot be read from it (it needs other evidence). (c) The price: a buyer and a seller must agree on a price at which the transaction takes place, so a sale cannot have happened without one even though the extract does not name it. (d) Either caption is defensible if justified: (i) rests on Paes's long list and the 'abundance of everything'; (ii) rests on Nuniz's craftsmen working in the streets where jewels and cloth were on sale. Marks go for a choice tied to words of the extract.
s: Part (a): grains and milk as needs, jewels and rubies as wants, with the definitions
Part (b): chooses goods-and-services availability and says the extract is silent on connecting people, traditions and ideas
Part (c): price named as the missing feature and why a sale needs an agreed price
Part (d): a caption chosen and justified from the extract

questions.q: True or False? 'Because Fernao Nuniz called Hampi a barren country, the chapter shows that the Hampi Bazaar had very few goods on sale.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Nuniz wrote that the country was barren and yet found it a mystery how there should be an abundance of everything in it. The bazaar had grains, oil, silk, animals, jewels and cloth in great quantity, so 'barren' described the land, not the market.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: Nuniz marvelled at the abundance in a barren land, so the bazaar was well stocked

questions.q: At a school fair Dhruv offers Rs 25 for the pen-holder that Alia has made, and he will not pay a rupee more. Alia says she will not sell it for less than Rs 35 because it cost her Rs 30 to make. They part without a sale. Which feature that every market needs did not come about between them?
questions.a: A price that both of them accept. Both want to trade and the pen-holder is there, but Rs 25 is below Alia's lowest and Rs 35 is above Dhruv's highest, so no price suits both and the sale cannot be completed.
o: A price that both sides accept
A buyer who is interested in the pen-holder
A seller who has the pen-holder to offer
A second buyer competing with Dhruv for it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A place can be called a market only if buyers and sellers meet there in person.
Reason (R): Goods and services become available to individuals, households and businesses through markets.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: R is a statement from the chapter, so it is true. A is false: the chapter says a market can be at a physical place or online, and buyers and sellers can transact from thousands of kilometres apart. R does not support the 'only in person' idea.

questions.q: Two shoppers buy the same notebook. Reena pays the Rs 120 marked on it at a fixed-price store. Sohan bargains at a weekly haat, starting at Rs 120 and settling at Rs 95. (a) In which purchase does the chapter's account of buyers and sellers 'negotiating until a mutually agreeable price is reached' show itself openly? (b) Reena never bargained. Does that mean no price was agreed in her purchase? Answer from the chapter's meaning of price.
questions.a: (a) Sohan's purchase at the haat: the seller's first price came down by bargaining until both accepted Rs 95. (b) No. Price is the amount at which a buyer is willing to buy and a seller is willing to sell. Reena was willing to buy at Rs 120 and the store was willing to sell at Rs 120, so a price was agreed; she simply accepted the seller's amount without negotiating. (That negotiation is less common in such shops is the chapter's own open question, so the reason is an inference.)
s: Part (a): the haat purchase, where bargaining reaches the agreed price
Part (b): Reena's payment shows both sides willing at Rs 120, so a price was agreed without bargaining

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the chapter term in Column B that describes it.
Column A: 1. Rs 50, the amount Aman and Bina both accept for a bookmark  2. A family buys a second television for its larger screen  3. A family buys drinking water for the day  4. An order placed on a phone from another city is delivered to the door
Column B: a. a want  b. price  c. a need  d. an online market
questions.a: Rs 50, the accepted amount, is the price; the larger-screen television is desired and not essential, so a want; drinking water is required to survive, so a need; an order on a phone delivered to the door is an online market. The wrong pairings swap need and want or confuse price with the market.

questions.q: Imran says, 'A market is only about money. Nothing else happens there.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. 'Only' is too strong. The chapter says markets supply goods and services that people need and want, and in addition markets connect people, traditions and ideas. So markets do more than move money.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the word 'only'
States that markets supply goods and services people need and want
States that markets also connect people, traditions and ideas

questions.q: Rekha is a tailor who stitches clothes in her shop. Mohan teaches mathematics online. Each charges Rs 400 a month. (a) Going by the chapter, which of the two can serve a customer thousands of kilometres away, and which cannot, and why? (b) Rekha's customers still make her shop a market. Name the three features that make it one.
questions.a: (a) Mohan can: the chapter names online classes as a service one can use without leaving home, with payment online. Rekha cannot: the chapter says services like tailoring require in-person contact and cannot be provided online. (b) A buyer (her customer), a seller (Rekha) and a price on which they agree (here Rs 400); the market is a physical one.
s: Part (a): Mohan's online service against Rekha's tailoring that needs in-person contact
Part (b): buyer, seller and agreed price named

questions.q:
A class runs a one-day stall. In the first hour 30 buyers purchase bottles of drinking water at Rs 10 each, but only 6 buy friendship bands at the asked price of Rs 60. The stall then lowers the band price to Rs 40 and 14 buy in the next hour.
(a) Classify water and bands as need or want.
(b) Work out the money taken from bands in each hour.
(c) What does the change in sales show about the price in a market, and what may have happened if the stall had refused to move below Rs 60?
(d) Name one thing these figures do not tell the class before it can say whether lowering the price was wise.
questions.a: (a) Water is a need (required to survive); bands are a want (desired, not essential). (b) 6 x 60 = Rs 360 in the first hour; 14 x 40 = Rs 560 in the next. (c) Price is the amount at which a buyer is willing to buy and a seller is willing to sell. Buyers found Rs 60 too high; at Rs 40 more were willing. If the stall had held at Rs 60, no price acceptable to both might have been reached and the sales might not have taken place. (d) The cost of making the bands, because the chapter says a seller will not sell at a price that is not profitable; more money taken does not show profit.
s: Part (a): water as need, bands as want
Part (b): Rs 360 and Rs 560
Part (c): price as the amount both accept, with the effect of holding at Rs 60
Part (d): cost or profit named as the missing information

questions.q: At a village fair, farmers from three villages explain their seed-saving methods to buyers while selling vegetables, and buyers from two communities share recipes with them. Which role of markets, named in the chapter, does this show best, in addition to supplying goods and services?
o: Markets connect people, traditions and ideas
Markets make goods and services available to households and businesses
Buyers and sellers agree on a price for each sale
Markets can be only at a physical place
questions.a: The chapter says that markets, besides supplying goods and services, connect people, traditions and ideas. The fair shows people from different places exchanging ideas while trading. The second option is also a role in the chapter but is the one the stem sets aside ('in addition to'); agreeing a price is a feature, not what the sharing of methods and recipes shows; and the chapter says a market can be physical or online, not 'only' physical.

questions.q: At a fair, Aman hands over Rs 50 and receives a handmade bookmark from Bina after the two have agreed on that amount. (a) Which part of the event is the trade and which is the price? (b) Why is price not the same thing as trade?
questions.a: (a) The exchange of the bookmark for the money is the trade (buying and selling); Rs 50 is the price. (b) Price is only the amount at which the buyer is willing to buy and the seller willing to sell; trade is the whole buying, selling or exchange of goods and services, which is completed once that price is agreed.
s: Part (a): exchange of bookmark for money as trade, Rs 50 as price
Part (b): price is the agreed amount, trade is the whole exchange it completes

questions.q: Describe a purchase at your school's annual-day fair in three or four sentences so that it shows a buyer, a seller and a price. Mark each of the three in your account.
questions.a: Any suitable account, e.g. 'Meera (buyer) asks Tarun (seller) for a bookmark. He asks Rs 20; she offers Rs 15; they settle at Rs 18, and she pays.' It must name a buyer, a seller and an agreed price.
s: A buyer clearly shown
A seller clearly shown
A price on which both agree, so the transaction is completed

questions.q:
Imtiaz sells dry fruits at a Sunday haat. About 40 customers come each week and the average bill is Rs 200; the dry fruit in that bill costs him Rs 140. A friend suggests he also sell on a shopping app. He expects 25 app orders a week from other cities at Rs 260 each. For each app order the goods cost him Rs 180, the app takes a commission of Rs 40 and packing and posting cost Rs 35. Packing takes him 8 extra hours a week.
(a) Which two features from the chapter make an app sale a market even though the buyer never visits his stall?
(b) An app buyer offers Rs 250 instead of Rs 260. Using the chapter's idea of the seller's side of price, should he accept? Work out his gain or loss per order at Rs 250.
(c) Work out his weekly profit from the haat and from the app at Rs 260.
(d) Decide whether he should add the app, using the figures and one point from the chapter other than money.
questions.a: (a) A buyer and a seller who agree on a price; the chapter says a market can be physical or online. (b) Cost per order = 180 + 40 + 35 = Rs 255, so at Rs 250 he loses Rs 5 per order. The chapter says a seller may not sell at a price that is not profitable, so he should refuse. (c) Haat: 40 x (200 - 140) = Rs 2,400. App: 25 x (260 - 255) = Rs 125. (d) Either choice can be defended. Add: the app earns an extra Rs 125 and reaches buyers in other cities who could never visit a haat. Do not add: Rs 125 for 8 hours is small and any rise in commission turns it into a loss. The answer must use Rs 125 and a non-money point such as reach or effort.
s: Part (a): buyer, seller and agreed price; online allowed
Part (b): Rs 255 cost, loss of Rs 5, seller will not sell unprofitably
Part (c): Rs 2,400 at the haat and Rs 125 on the app
Part (d): a decision using Rs 125 and a non-money point

questions.q: Two farmers swap 10 kg of rice for 12 kg of jowar without any money changing hands, while at the Sunday haat a third farmer sells 10 kg of rice for money. Ritu says, 'The chapter's word is buying and selling, so a swap is not trade at all.' (a) Use the chapter's glossary meaning of 'trade' to say whether she is right. (b) Why does the word 'price' in the chapter fit the haat sale more directly than the swap?
questions.a: (a) No, Ritu is wrong. The glossary defines trade as buying and selling or exchange of goods and services between people or countries, so the swap is trade. (b) The chapter defines price as the amount at which a buyer is willing to buy and a seller is willing to sell, and a market transaction is described as a buyer paying an agreed price; in the haat sale that amount is in rupees, while in the swap the farmers agree on quantities and no money amount is named. This second point is an inference from the chapter's wording.
s: Part (a): the swap is trade because trade includes exchange of goods
Part (b): price is the agreed amount at which the buyer buys and the seller sells, clearest where money changes hands (inference)

questions.q: Compare the Hampi Bazaar of the 16th century with an online shopping app of today. State what is common to both and what is different, and then say what this tells you about the features of any market.
questions.a: Common: each has buyers and sellers, goods, and a price to be agreed, and each connects people. Different: Hampi was a physical place where buyers met sellers face to face, while an app lets them transact from thousands of kilometres apart with goods delivered to the doorstep and payment online. So the essential features are a buyer, a seller and an agreed price, while the place can be physical or online.
s: Common features: buyer, seller, price
Differences: face to face against online and delivery
Conclusion about the essential features of a market

questions.q: Aman says, 'A market supplies the goods people need, like the grains of Hampi. Wants like rubies and silk are not its business, and bringing people or traditions together has nothing to do with a market.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. He is right that a market supplies needs: Hampi sold grains and milk. But the chapter says people have relied on markets to fulfil their needs and their wants, and Hampi also sold jewels and silk, so wants are the market's business too. And the chapter adds that markets connect people, traditions and ideas, so that part of his claim is wrong.
s: Verdict: agrees only partly, since one part holds
Accepts that markets supply needs, but wants too, with the Hampi goods as examples
Rejects 'nothing to do with bringing people together': markets connect people, traditions and ideas

questions.q: A seller bought 100 kg of guavas at Rs 35 per kg and spends Rs 700 more that day on carrying them and running his stall. If he sells all 100 kg, the least price per kg at which he avoids a loss is Rs ___.

Mahesh bought tomatoes at Rs 35 per kg. Buyers keep walking away at Rs 60 per kg, but at Rs 45 per kg his stock sold out. A friend urges him to drop the price to Rs 10 per kg 'so that everyone buys'. What is the main problem with that advice?
o: He would make a loss, as that price is not profitable for him
Buyers would suspect poor quality and would not buy at all
He would lose his customers to a rival seller
Buyers would stop trusting him because the price keeps changing
questions.a: The chapter says a seller may not agree to a price that is not profitable for him, and a price that is too low means he loses. Rs 10 is far below his cost of Rs 35, so every kilogram he sold would lose him Rs 25. The other three are slips: the chapter says nothing about buyers suspecting quality, about a rival, or about distrust from changing prices.

questions.q:
A guava seller bought at Rs 35 per kg and will not sell below Rs 40 per kg. A buyer is ready to pay at most Rs 45 per kg.
1. A sale at Rs 38 per kg can take place, because it is above the Rs 35 the seller paid.
2. A sale at Rs 42 per kg can take place, because both sides are willing to accept it.
3. A sale at Rs 48 per kg can take place, because the seller would gain more and the buyer will have to agree.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: A price works only if it is acceptable to both sides. Rs 42 lies between the seller's lowest price (Rs 40) and the buyer's highest (Rs 45), so statement 2 is correct. Rs 38 is below what the seller will accept, and Rs 48 is above what the buyer will pay, so statements 1 and 3 are false.

questions.q: True or False? 'If the seller of guavas fixes a very low price, every buyer is happy, so a very low price is also a good price for the market.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. A very low price is not profitable for the seller and he may lose money. The chapter's good price is one that is just right: high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. A price that suits one side only does not settle the market.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: a very low price is not profitable for the seller; the price must suit both sides

questions.q: A guava seller is planning how many kilograms to bring to his stall next Saturday. Which of these pieces of information would NOT help him judge roughly how many kilograms buyers need, going by the chapter?
o: The price at which the farmer sold him guavas last season
How many kg were left unsold at the end of each Saturday evening
How fast his stock sold out when he asked Rs 40 per kg
How many buyers walked away when he asked Rs 80 per kg of guavas
questions.a: The chapter says the seller learns from how buyers respond at different prices and so assesses approximately what quantity buyers need. Unsold stock, speed of sale and walk-aways all show buyers' response. What the farmer charged last season shows nothing about how many kilograms buyers need.

questions.q:
For one weekly market, guava sellers and buyers behave as below.
At Rs 60 per kg: sellers offer 200 kg, buyers need 120 kg.
At Rs 40 per kg: sellers offer 150 kg, buyers need 150 kg.
At Rs 30 per kg: sellers offer 90 kg, buyers need 170 kg.
Which price fits the chapter's idea of a price that is just right?
o: Rs 40, where the amount offered matches the amount needed
Rs 60, where sellers would earn the most on each kilogram
Rs 30, where buyers would need the largest number of kilograms
Rs 45, which is simply the average of the three prices
questions.a: The chapter says the amount of goods offered by sellers and the amount required by buyers help determine the price that is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. At Rs 40 the 150 kg offered is exactly what buyers need. At Rs 60 sellers have 80 kg more than buyers want, at Rs 30 buyers are short of 80 kg, and an average is not a price anyone has tested.

questions.q:
Anwar buys guavas from a farmer at Rs 30 per kg. On four Saturdays he brought 100 kg each time and tried a different price. Unsold guavas spoil and have to be thrown away.
Saturday 1: price Rs 80 per kg, 10 kg sold.
Saturday 2: price Rs 60 per kg, 35 kg sold.
Saturday 3: price Rs 50 per kg, 70 kg sold.
Saturday 4: price Rs 40 per kg, 100 kg sold.
This Saturday a rival seller has set up across the road and is asking Rs 40 per kg.
(a) At which price did his whole stock sell, and what does the chapter call a price that is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer?
(b) What was his loss on Saturday 1, counting the cost of all 100 kg he bought?
(c) What can Anwar learn from how the quantity sold changed as the price fell?
(d) With the rival at Rs 40, should Anwar bring 100 kg and match Rs 40, or bring about 70 kg and ask Rs 50 as on Saturday 3? Work out his profit in each case if his earlier sales repeat, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) At Rs 40, where all 100 kg sold (this shows buyers wanted at least 100 kg at that price); the chapter calls such a price one that is just right. (b) Receipts 10 x 80 = Rs 800; cost 100 x 30 = Rs 3,000; loss Rs 2,200. (c) The seller can assess approximately what quantity buyers need at each price and offer that quantity in the market in future. (d) Matching Rs 40 with 100 kg: 100 x 10 = Rs 1,000 profit if all sell. Rs 50 with 70 kg: 70 x 20 = Rs 1,400 profit if those buyers still come. Either can be defended. Rs 50 earns Rs 400 more only if the buyers of Saturday 3 do not move to the rival; Rs 40 earns less but is the price at which buyers already showed they will buy the whole quantity, and the rival's presence makes the Saturday 3 sales uncertain. A good answer uses both figures and the risk from the rival.
s: Part (a): Rs 40 where the whole stock sold, and the 'just right' price
Part (b): a loss of Rs 2,200
Part (c): the seller assesses the quantity buyers need from their response and offers that
Part (d): Rs 1,000 and Rs 1,400 compared, with a choice that weighs the rival

questions.q: For three Saturdays, Sunil's guavas at Rs 40 per kg sold out by noon. His friend says, 'Everything sold, so Rs 40 is too low. Raise it to Rs 80 and you will earn double.' Which reply fits the chapter best?
questions.a: The chapter says that if a buyer finds the price very high he will ask for a lower one, and buyers may not be willing to buy at that price. The sell-outs show that buyers took everything at Rs 40, not that they will take it at Rs 80. The chapter does not say that a sell-out lets a seller name any price, that the government approves it, or that a price must stay fixed; the seller can learn from buyers' response and adjust the quantity.
o: At Rs 80 buyers may not buy, as in the chapter's first scenario; the sell-out is a cue to test
The friend is right, because a sell-out shows buyers will pay any price that a seller names
The friend is right, but only once the government has approved a higher price for guavas
The friend is wrong, because the chapter says a seller must keep one price on every day

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the guava example of the chapter the price settles near Rs 40 per kg, not at Rs 80 or Rs 20.
Reason (R): Over time, the amount of goods offered by the sellers and the amount required by the buyers help determine a price that is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both come from the chapter. At Rs 80 buyers hesitate and at Rs 20 the seller finds it unprofitable. The price that is just right comes from the amount sellers offer and buyers need, so R explains why it settles near Rs 40.

questions.q: The chapter asks why vegetables are sold cheaper late at night at the weekly market than during the day. (a) Using the idea that a price must suit both seller and buyer, suggest one reason why sellers accept lower prices late at night. (b) Why can the price not fall to any level whatever, even at that hour?
questions.a: (a) This is a reasoned inference, since the chapter only asks the question. Sellers who still have unsold vegetables late at night are better off at a lower price than with stock nobody buys, and the few remaining buyers will pay only the lower price, so a price both accept is lower. (b) The chapter says a seller may not be willing to sell at a price that is not profitable for him, so the price cannot go below what he can accept.
s: Part (a): a reasoned explanation based on unsold stock and a price both sides accept, marked as inference
Part (b): a seller will not sell at a price that is not profitable

questions.q: At Rs 40 per kg Ritu would like to buy 5 kg of guavas, but she has only Rs 120 with her. By the chapter's meaning of demand (the quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at a particular price), what is Ritu's demand for guavas at Rs 40?
questions.a: 3 kg. She is willing to buy 5 kg but able to pay for only 3 kg (Rs 120 divided by Rs 40), and the chapter's demand counts what consumers are both willing and able to purchase. Wanting 5 kg is not demand for 5 kg.
o: 3 kg
5 kg
0 kg, because she cannot pay for all she wants
1 kg, the amount that Rs 40 alone would buy

questions.q: A shoe seller buys a pair of sports shoes for Rs 1,100. On the first day he asks Rs 1,800 and buyers walk past; on the second day he asks Rs 1,400 and sells the pair. (a) Which of the chapter's three guava scenarios does the first day match, and what did the second day teach him? (b) Could he have gone down to Rs 900 to sell faster? Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) The first day matches the very high price: buyers may not buy at a price they find very high. The second day taught him roughly what price buyers will accept. (b) No. At Rs 900 he would lose Rs 200 on the pair, and the chapter says a seller may not be willing to sell at a price that is not profitable for him.
s: Part (a): very high price, buyers do not buy; the lower price shows what buyers accept
Part (b): Rs 900 is below his cost of Rs 1,100 so it is not profitable

questions.q: A buyer will pay at most Rs 30 per kg for guavas, but the seller has bought them at Rs 35 per kg and says he will not sell below that. Show that no deal can be made, and say what the chapter says about this situation.
questions.a: The buyer's highest price (Rs 30) is Rs 5 below the least the seller can accept (Rs 35), so no price is acceptable to both. The chapter says that if buyer and seller cannot reach a price both agree on, the transaction may not take place.
s: Compares Rs 30 and Rs 35, a gap of Rs 5
Concludes no price suits both
Links to the chapter: no agreed price, no transaction

questions.q: At the same market two guava sellers, both of whom bought at Rs 35 per kg, ask Rs 50 and Rs 42. By closing time the first has sold 8 kg and the second 60 kg. (a) What does each result tell its seller about the price that is just right? (b) Why can the second seller not simply drop to Rs 34 to sell still more?
questions.a: (a) The first seller learns that many buyers found Rs 50 too high, so he must come down towards what buyers accept (the first scenario of the chapter); the second learns that buyers accepted Rs 42, so it is close to a price that suits both sides. That a rival's lower price drew buyers away is an inference. (b) At Rs 34 he would lose Re 1 on each kilogram, below his cost of Rs 35, and the chapter says a seller may not be willing to sell at a price that is not profitable for him.
s: Part (a): Rs 50 found too high by buyers; Rs 42 accepted by buyers (inference about the rival)
Part (b): Rs 34 is below his cost of Rs 35, so not profitable

questions.q: Onions are an important part of Indian cooking. In some seasons their supply to the market falls, and in some a very large crop arrives. Using the chapter's idea that price comes from the amount sellers offer and buyers need, reason out what is likely to happen to the price in each case, and say why the seller cannot fix any price he likes.
questions.a: When supply falls and buyers still need onions, there is less to go around, so the price is likely to rise. When a very large crop arrives and buyers need only so much, sellers have more than buyers need, so the price is likely to fall. This is an inference from the chapter's idea. The seller cannot fix any price he likes because buyers may not buy at a very high price, and a very low price would not be profitable for him; the price has to be acceptable to both.
s: Fall in supply and the likely rise in price
Very large supply and the likely fall in price
Ties each to amount offered against amount needed
Very high price: buyers may not buy
Very low price: not profitable for the seller

questions.q: Hema says, 'The just-right price for guavas is high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer, and a seller reaches it by himself on the first day, by thinking about his own cost.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. The first half is right: the chapter describes a price that is just right as high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. The second half is wrong: the chapter says the price is determined over time by the amount of goods offered by sellers and the amount required by buyers, and the seller learns it from how buyers respond, so cost alone on day one does not settle it.
s: Verdict: agrees only partly
Accepts the description of a just-right price: high enough for the seller, low enough for the buyer
Rejects 'by himself on the first day': the price is determined over time by the amount offered and the amount needed

questions.q: A roadside stall sells mangoes at Rs 90 per kg and refuses to bargain, saying a lower price would be a loss. A family instead pays Rs 130 per kg for mangoes sold in a neat sealed box at a shopping mall. Give two reasons, not connected to price, for the family's choice: one about what the seller offers and one about the buyer's own convenience.
questions.a: One reason about the seller's offer, such as neat sealed packing, a clean shop or trusted quality; and one about the buyer's convenience, such as no bargaining or argument, or everything available at one place. Price is not the only factor in buying and selling.
s: A valid non-price reason about what the seller offers
A valid non-price reason about the buyer's convenience

questions.q:
A shop in Shimla bought 100 woollen sweaters at Rs 600 each. It sold them in three stages.
November-December: price Rs 1,000, 40 sweaters sold.
January: price Rs 800, 35 sweaters sold.
Late February, when winter was ending: price Rs 550, the last 25 sweaters sold.
(a) The chapter gives two ideas about price: buyers may not buy at a price they find very high, and a seller may refuse a price that is not profitable. Which of the two best explains why the shop kept lowering its price after January? Give a likely reason.
(b) At Rs 550 the shop sold below its cost. Work out the loss per sweater and in all.
(c) Work out the total profit on all 100 sweaters.
(d) Before the late-February sale the owner wondered whether to store the last 25 sweaters and sell them next winter at Rs 1,000 each. Give one point for and one against, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The first: buyers do not buy at a price they find too high. The likely reason (the chapter only asks 'why does this happen?') is that buyers' need for woollens falls as winter ends, so the price buyers accept falls with it; this is an inference. (b) Rs 600 - Rs 550 = Rs 50 per sweater; 25 x 50 = Rs 1,250 in all. (c) 40 x 400 = 16,000; 35 x 200 = 7,000; less 1,250 gives Rs 21,750. (d) For: Rs 550 is below cost, so waiting may bring a better price when buyers need woollens again. Against: the shop holds stock with no money coming in, and buyers' need is low now, so it may not find buyers soon.
s: Part (a): buyers do not buy at a high price; need for woollens falls after winter (inference)
Part (b): Rs 50 per sweater and Rs 1,250 in all
Part (c): total profit Rs 21,750
Part (d): one point for and one against, linked to buyers' need after winter

questions.q: Write a four-line dialogue between a buyer and a seller of mangoes in which the seller's first price is brought down to a price both accept. Mention the first price, the counter-offer and the final price.
questions.a: Any dialogue with the seller's first price, the buyer's lower counter-offer, and a final price in between at which the sale happens, e.g. Rs 120, Rs 90, Rs 100.
s: Seller's first price stated
Buyer's lower counter-offer stated
Final price between the two, with the sale made

questions.q:
A seller buys guavas from a farmer at Rs 30 per kg and has sold 100 kg every Saturday at Rs 40 per kg. Pleased with the profit, he asks the farmer for 150 kg next Saturday at the same Rs 30. Buyers actually need about 110 kg at Rs 40.
(a) What is his weekly profit on 100 kg?
(b) What is his result if he orders 150 kg and only 110 kg sell at Rs 40, with the rest wasted?
(c) Which idea from the chapter did he forget, and what should he do before ordering again?
(d) How may the farmer's thinking about next season change after this?
questions.a: (a) 100 x 40 - 100 x 30 = 4,000 - 3,000 = Rs 1,000. (b) 110 x 40 = 4,400 received against 150 x 30 = 4,500 spent: a loss of Rs 100. (c) The seller must assess approximately what quantity buyers need from their response and offer that quantity; more guavas than buyers need earn nothing. He should order near what sold out and test before raising it. (d) This is an inference from the chapter's idea: the farmer too will watch how much buyers need, and not simply grow more because one buyer wants more, since the amount offered and the amount needed together decide the price.
s: Part (a): Rs 1,000
Part (b): a loss of Rs 100 on 110 kg sold
Part (c): assess the quantity buyers need and offer that quantity
Part (d): the farmer would think about demand, marked as an inference

questions.q: Seema's father wants to buy a television and prefers to see it before paying; her mother prefers to order it on a shopping app. (a) Give one point from the chapter that supports each parent. (b) For which would the choice of an online market be worse: the television or a blouse that Seema's tailor must stitch to her measurements? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Father: in a physical market the buyer can meet the seller physically. Mother: on an app, goods such as TVs are delivered to the doorstep and the buyer need not travel. (b) The blouse: tailoring needs in-person contact and cannot be provided online.
s: Part (a): one point for each parent from the chapter
Part (b): the blouse, because tailoring needs in-person contact

questions.q: A Tirupur company orders cotton yarn on a shopping website from a seller in Coimbatore and uses it to make T-shirts that it sells to shops. Which pairing is correct in the chapter's terms?
o: The yarn is an input for production; the company a manufacturer
The yarn is a finished good for it; the company is an aggregator
The yarn is an export for it; the company is a distributor
The yarn is an input for production; the company is an importer
questions.a: Materials used to make goods are inputs for production, and a person or company that makes goods for sale is a manufacturer. The website, not the company, is the aggregator, and nothing in the case crosses a border, so import or export does not arise.

questions.q:
A Kochi food company buys palm oil each quarter. Its orders were: Malaysia 2,400 tonnes at Rs 90,000 per tonne; Indonesia 3,600 tonnes at Rs 88,000 per tonne; Thailand 1,000 tonnes at Rs 95,000 per tonne. The company also sells packed biscuits to a shop in Dubai. A Kerala supplier now offers palm oil at Rs 94,000 per tonne.
(a) Which of the two sources for next quarter, Indonesia or the Kerala supplier, would be a domestic market, and which term describes the company's role as buyer in the other?
(b) What term describes the sale of biscuits to Dubai from the company's side?
(c) What did the Indonesian order cost, in crore rupees?
(d) For next quarter's 3,600 tonnes, should the company buy from Indonesia or from the Kerala supplier? Decide, using the price difference and one point about domestic and international markets.
questions.a: (a) The Kerala supplier is a domestic market (buyer and seller inside India); buying from Indonesia is an international market, where the company is an importer (import). (b) Export. (c) 3,600 x 88,000 = Rs 31,68,00,000 = Rs 31.68 crore. (d) Indonesia is Rs 6,000 per tonne cheaper, so 3,600 x 6,000 = Rs 2.16 crore less. Either choice can be argued: Indonesia saves money; the Kerala supplier keeps the trade inside India's boundaries (a domestic market) with no import across a border. This is a judgement; the chapter says only that most palm oil is imported from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
s: Part (a): Kerala as domestic, Indonesia as international with the company importing
Part (b): export
Part (c): Rs 31.68 crore
Part (d): a decision using the Rs 2.16 crore difference and a point on domestic or international markets

questions.q: Four places are described. Going by the chapter's meaning of an aggregator (a website or mobile application that organizes and combines offers from multiple sellers and sells them to consumers at one place), which one is an aggregator?
questions.a: A shopping app that lists the offers of two hundred small sellers on one screen and sells them to consumers. A mall is a multi-storey building with many stores but it is a physical market, and a haat is physical too. A single shop's own website carries the offers of only one seller, so it does not combine offers from multiple sellers.
o: A shopping app listing the offers of many sellers at one place
A mall in which two hundred stores sell their goods under one roof
A shop's own website that sells only the goods that the shop makes
A weekly haat in which two hundred vendors sell their goods from carts

questions.q: Karan says, 'When a Surat saree maker sells sarees to a shop in Jaipur, it is an export, because the sarees leave Surat.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter's meaning of export.
questions.a: Not at all. Export means selling goods or services produced in one country to a buyer in another country. Jaipur is inside India, so the sale takes place within the boundaries of the country and is a domestic market transaction. Leaving a city is not the same as crossing a country's border.
s: Verdict: disagrees entirely
Meaning of export: sale to a buyer in another country
Jaipur is inside India, so the sale is domestic

questions.q: A Surat saree maker sells 900 sarees at Rs 1,500 each to a shop in Jaipur and 600 sarees at Rs 2,000 each to a shop in Dubai. Her earnings from exports are Rs ___ lakh (write a number).
True or False? 'Online classes can be taken without leaving home, so every service can be moved from a physical market to an online market.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says some services, such as tailoring, need in-person contact and cannot be provided online. Online classes are one example of a service that can be bought online, but they do not make every service suitable.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: services needing in-person contact, like tailoring, cannot be provided online

questions.q:
A village family lives 30 km from a town. A bus round trip costs Rs 100 for one adult, and one adult travels. Each month they need groceries and books, which cost the same online as in town; an online order carries Rs 80 delivery. In 4 months of the year a blouse must also be stitched in town, because the village tailor cannot do that cut, and tailoring needs in-person contact. Compare three rules for the year: Rule X, always buy in town; Rule Y, always order online and make the trip as well in the 4 tailoring months; Rule Z, order online in the 8 other months and shop in town on the trip in the 4 tailoring months.
(a) Which of their needs can an online market meet and which can it not, according to the chapter?
(b) What do they spend on travel and delivery in a year under Rule X and under Rule Y?
(c) What do they spend under Rule Z, and how much does it save against Rule X?
(d) In which months does online beat the town, and in which does it not?
(e) Advise the family on one rule, giving one reason from the figures and one point about what a buyer can or cannot do in an online market.
questions.a: (a) Groceries and books can be bought online and delivered to the doorstep; the stitching needs in-person contact and cannot be provided online. (b) Rule X: 12 x 100 = Rs 1,200. Rule Y: 4 x (80 + 100) + 8 x 80 = 720 + 640 = Rs 1,360. (c) Rule Z: 4 x 100 + 8 x 80 = 400 + 640 = Rs 1,040, which saves Rs 160 against Rule X. (d) In the 8 months with no tailoring trip, online costs Rs 80 against Rs 100, so it saves Rs 20 a month; in the 4 tailoring months the trip is made anyway, so shopping in town costs nothing extra and online adds Rs 80. (e) Rule Z is cheapest by the figures. A family may still prefer Rule X if it values seeing the books or choosing vegetables in person: the chapter says in a physical market the buyer can meet the seller physically, whereas online goods arrive at the doorstep. Any reasoned recommendation using the figures is accepted.
s: Part (a): goods can be bought online, tailoring needs in-person contact
Part (b): Rs 1,200 under Rule X and Rs 1,360 under Rule Y
Part (c): Rs 1,040 under Rule Z and a saving of Rs 160
Part (d): online wins in the 8 months with no trip, loses in the 4 tailoring months
Part (e): a recommendation using the figures and a physical-or-online point

questions.q: Gauri says, 'The share market is not really a market, because nobody buys or sells goods or services there.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: It is another kind of market, one that does not transact goods or services
She is right, because the chapter says every market must sell some goods
She is right, because the chapter treats the share market as domestic only
It is a physical market like a haat, because buyers and sellers meet there
questions.a: The chapter names the share or stock market as one of the other types of markets that do not transact goods and services. So being a market does not depend on selling goods. The other options make claims that the chapter does not.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The paper used to print the Class 7 textbook was bought in a domestic market.
Reason (R): Domestic markets exist outside a nation's boundary.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: the paper came from big paper mills located all over India, so buyer and seller were inside the country. R is false: a domestic market is within the geographical boundaries of the country, and it is international markets that exist outside a nation's boundary.

questions.q: A Pune family orders a pair of shoes on an app from a seller in Agra. 'Physical or online' and 'domestic or international' are two different ways of sorting markets. (a) Sort this purchase on both scales. (b) Could the same shoes be bought in a physical, domestic market? Say what would change.
questions.a: (a) Online (bought through an app, delivered) and domestic (buyer and seller are both inside India). (b) Yes: if the family bought them in a shop or mall in Pune, it would be a physical market, still domestic. The buyer would meet the seller and carry the shoes home instead of having them delivered.
s: Part (a): online and domestic
Part (b): physical but still domestic, with the buyer meeting the seller

questions.q: Surat's cotton cloth makers receive raw cotton through cotton mandis, which are physical markets. Show that the statement 'inputs for production can be bought only in a physical market' cannot be true, using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says that manufacturers can also buy components online to be used as inputs for production. So at least one kind of input purchase happens in an online market, and 'only' fails. The Surat cotton arriving through mandis shows physical markets do supply inputs, but one online example is enough to disprove 'only'.
s: Names the Surat cotton mandi as a physical source of inputs
States that manufacturers can buy components online as inputs
Concludes that one online example is enough to disprove 'only'

questions.q:
Read the statements about markets.
1. A weekly haat and a multi-storey mall are both physical markets, where the buyer can meet the seller physically.
2. Manufacturers can also buy components online to be used as inputs for production.
3. The paper bought by the printers of the textbook from mills located all over India was an international purchase, because the mills are far from the press.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: a market within the geographical boundaries of the country is a domestic market, however far apart buyer and seller are inside it; the chapter uses this very paper as its example of a domestic transaction.

questions.q:
The library of a Nagpur school needs 60 copies of a reading book before its Reading Week begins in 10 days. A local bookshop offers them at Rs 240 each, ready to collect today. A shopping app run by an aggregator offers Rs 210 each plus Rs 450 for delivery of the whole order, with delivery promised in 8 days.
(a) Which offer is in a physical market and which in an online market? State how the books reach the school in each.
(b) The app is run by an aggregator. Using the chapter's meaning of the word, say what an aggregator does that the single local bookshop does not.
(c) How much would the library save by using the app?
(d) Choose between the two and justify, using one point about money and one about the nature of the physical or online market.
questions.a: (a) The bookshop is a physical market: the school collects the books in person. The app is an online market: the books are delivered to the doorstep. (b) An aggregator is a website or mobile application that organises and combines offers from multiple sellers and sells them to consumers at one place; the local bookshop offers only its own stock. (c) Bookshop 60 x 240 = Rs 14,400; app 60 x 210 + 450 = Rs 13,050; saving Rs 1,350. (d) Either may be defended: the app saves Rs 1,350 and delivers to the doorstep, but delivery leaves only 2 days of margin; the bookshop costs more but the books can be checked in person and collected today, so there is no risk of delay.
s: Part (a): bookshop physical, collected in person; app online, doorstep delivery
Part (b): aggregator combines offers from many sellers at one place, unlike the single bookshop
Part (c): Rs 1,350 saved
Part (d): a choice backed by the saving and the physical or online nature of the market

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the term in Column B that describes it.
Column A: 1. A customer picks a pair of shoes from a store inside a city mall  2. A TV ordered on a phone is delivered to the buyer's door  3. A Delhi company sells software services to a client in Canada  4. A Chennai company buys palm oil from Indonesia
Column B: a. an import for the buyer  b. an export for the seller  c. a physical market  d. an online market
questions.a: A mall store is a physical market; an order on a phone delivered to the door is an online market; selling services to a buyer in another country is an export; buying palm oil from Indonesia is an import. The wrong pairings swap import with export or physical with online.

questions.q: A potter sells earthen lamps at the weekly haat of his town and is thinking of selling them on a shopping app as well. (a) Give one gain and one loss for the potter as a seller if he moves entirely online. (b) Give one gain and one loss for a buyer who changes from the haat to the app.
questions.a: (a) Gain: buyers far away can buy from him, thousands of kilometres from his town. Loss: he no longer meets the buyer, as a seller at the haat does. (b) Gain: the lamps are delivered to the doorstep without the buyer travelling. Loss: the buyer cannot meet the seller or see the lamps physically before paying. Any gain and loss that follows from the chapter's physical and online descriptions is accepted.
s: Part (a): one gain and one loss for the seller
Part (b): one gain and one loss for the buyer

questions.q: Write a short situation, in three or four sentences, in which a customer cannot be served by an online market even though the seller has a good app. Name the service, say why it cannot be given online and say where the customer must go instead.
questions.a: Any suitable situation, e.g. a customer wants a school uniform stitched to her measurements. Tailoring needs in-person contact, so it cannot be provided online, and she must go to a physical market, the tailor's shop. The service must be one needing in-person contact.
s: A service needing in-person contact named
Reason: it needs in-person contact, so cannot be given online
The customer goes to a physical market

questions.q: Fig. 12.10 of the chapter shows, region by region, what India exports and what India imports. Its West Asia entries are refined petroleum products, crude petroleum and fertilizers. It names items only and gives no quantities or rupee values. Which claim about India's dealings with West Asia can NOT be drawn from the figure alone?
questions.a: The figure lists items but no amounts, so nothing in it says how much petroleum or fertilizer moves; the claim about 'more' cannot be drawn. The other three can: refined and crude petroleum are listed for West Asia, fertilizers are listed for West Asia, and because West Asia is outside India the dealings cross borders (an international market). The figure's direction labels are not needed for any of these.
o: Both sides trade more with West Asia in petroleum than in fertilizers
Petroleum products are among the goods India trades with West Asia
Fertilizers are among the goods India trades with West Asia
India's dealings with West Asia are across country borders

questions.q:
A student writes, 'India was the world's largest importer of vegetable oils in 2024, so India must have no domestic market for vegetable oils.' Using the chapter, decide whether the conclusion follows.
(a) Apply the chapter's meaning of domestic and international markets to two deals: a Kerala farmer sells pepper to a Mumbai trader, and a Delhi firm buys sunflower oil from a seller abroad. State what each deal is and why.
(b) State what the chapter says about India's vegetable oil imports in 2024.
(c) Say whether any of this shows that there is no domestic market, and what the student would need to know.
questions.a: (a) The pepper deal is in a domestic market, because buyer and seller are both within the geographical boundaries of the country, as with the paper bought from mills all over India. The sunflower oil deal is in an international market: the Delhi firm is a buyer importing a product produced in another country, so trade crosses the border. (b) India was the world's largest importer of vegetable oils like palm, sunflower and soybean oil in 2024, and most of the palm oil is imported from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. (c) The conclusion does not follow. Being the largest importer says India buys a great deal from abroad; it does not say how much is bought inside India or that no oil is. The chapter gives no figure for oil bought inside India, so the student would need that figure before concluding anything.
s: Part (a): pepper deal as domestic, with the within-the-country reason
Part (a): oil deal as international, an import across the border
Part (b): the 2024 largest-importer fact and the three palm-oil sources
Part (c): the conclusion does not follow
Part (c): says what extra information is needed, since the chapter gives no domestic figure

questions.q: A Bengaluru firm writes software for a client in Canada and is paid online. (a) Is this an import or an export for the Bengaluru firm, and which for the Canadian client? (b) Explain how one deal can be called by two different names.
questions.a: (a) An export for the Bengaluru firm (it sells a service produced in India to a buyer in another country) and an import for the Canadian client (it buys a service from another country and brings it into its own). (b) The name depends on which side is speaking: the seller's side calls the deal an export and the buyer's side calls the same deal an import, because trade occurs across the borders of countries.
s: Part (a): export for the firm, import for the client
Part (b): seller's side says export and buyer's side says import for the same deal

questions.q: Pooja's mother buys 2 kg of grapes from a fruit cart near their flats. Which sequence best describes the path of those grapes from the vineyard, in the chapter's physical-market chain?
o: Producer, wholesaler (godown or cold store), mandi, retailer, consumer
Producer, retailer, mandi, wholesaler (godown or cold store), consumer
Producer, aggregator, wholesaler, distributor, mandi, consumer
Producer, mandi, aggregator, retailer, wholesaler, final consumer
questions.a: In a physical market the chapter has wholesalers buy from the farms, store the produce in godowns (cold storage for perishables such as grapes), bring it to the mandi, and supply the retailers near households, who sell to the final consumer. A retailer cannot come before the wholesaler, and the aggregator belongs to the online chain.

questions.q: A dyeing unit in Surat buys woven fabric at Rs 90 per metre and sells dyed fabric at Rs 130 per metre. In a week it dyes 5,000 metres. (a) In which two markets of the Surat chain does it deal, and in which role in each? (b) How much more does it receive than it spends on the fabric in the week, and what must that amount cover?
questions.a: (a) It is a buyer in the market for woven fabric and a seller in the market for dyed fabric. (b) 5,000 x (130 - 90) = Rs 2,00,000. This has to cover the dyeing work (dyes, wages, power) and leave the unit something to keep.
s: Part (a): buyer in the woven-fabric market, seller in the dyed-fabric market
Part (b): Rs 2,00,000 and the dyeing costs it must cover

questions.q:
Read the statements about the supply of goods.
1. A dyeing unit in Surat buys woven fabric in one market and sells dyed fabric in the next, so cotton passes through several markets before it reaches the final consumer.
2. Retailers buy from wholesalers mainly so that they can resell the goods to other retailers.
3. In an online market, the aggregator hands each order to a wholesaler, who then delivers it to the buyer.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
questions.a: Only statement 1 is in the chapter: the product moves from one stage to another through markets for woven fabric, dyed fabric and finished products. Statement 2 is false: retailers sell in smaller quantities and the goods are meant for consumption. Statement 3 is false: the aggregator itself packs the products and delivers them to the online buyer.

questions.q: A Surat wholesaler holds 6,000 saree pieces. Forty-five retailers each ask for 140 pieces. Show by calculation that the wholesaler cannot meet every order, and say what the chapter suggests wholesalers do to avoid such a gap.
questions.a: 45 x 140 = 6,300 pieces are wanted but only 6,000 are held, so 300 pieces are short. The chapter says wholesalers assess how much product retailers need, which helps maintain stock with the manufacturers and ensures uninterrupted supply.
s: Total demanded: 6,300
Shortage of 300 pieces
Wholesalers assess retailers' requirements to keep stock

questions.q: A retailer buys tomatoes at Rs 18 per kg and sells them at Rs 25 per kg. His shop costs him Rs 700 on a day. To cover that cost from the difference between his buying and selling prices he must sell at least ___ kg.

A hill-village shopkeeper says, 'We do not need wholesalers. Manufacturers should send goods straight to every shop.' Use the chapter to evaluate this.
(a) What do wholesalers do in a physical market?
(b) What do wholesalers in Surat do that helps the manufacturers?
(c) Where does the chapter show goods going from the manufacturer to a seller without a wholesaler, and who takes over the next stage there?
(d) Give your verdict for the village shops.
questions.a: (a) Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers or manufacturers, store them in godowns (with cold storage for perishables) and supply the shops near households. (b) They assess how much product retailers need, which helps maintain the stock of products with the manufacturers and ensures an uninterrupted supply to consumers. (c) In online markets, manufacturers send bulk quantities to the aggregator's warehouse, and the aggregator packs and delivers. (d) A reasoned verdict: for scattered shops in hills, the chapter says even wholesalers find it hard to reach many retailers because of distance and terrain, so distributors are needed; a manufacturer sending goods to every shop would meet the same difficulty without the wholesaler's storage and stock assessment. Direct supply can work only where something like an aggregator handles the packing and delivery.
s: Part (a): bulk buying, storage in godowns, supply to shops
Part (b): assessing retailers' needs to keep stock with manufacturers
Part (c): the online chain, with the aggregator packing and delivering
Part (d): a verdict with at least one reason from the chapter

questions.q: A town has four businesses that sell to others. A salon serves families who live nearby, a cinema hall sells tickets to the public, a neighbourhood restaurant serves meals, and a mandi trader sells tomatoes by the truckload to shopkeepers. Which one is NOT a retail store in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: The mandi trader: he sells in bulk to shopkeepers who will resell, which is wholesale. The chapter says retail stores also exist for services like salons, movie theatres and restaurants, selling to final consumers near households, so the other three are retail.
o: The mandi trader selling tomatoes by the truckload to shopkeepers
The salon that serves families who live in the nearby lanes
The cinema hall that sells tickets to the public every evening
The neighbourhood restaurant serving meals to local families

questions.q:
A group of farmers near Nashik has 500 kg of tomatoes this week. The wholesaler buys from farmers at Rs 9 per kg and sells to retailers at Rs 18 per kg, and the retailers sell to consumers at Rs 25 per kg. A weekly market in town will buy up to 300 kg at Rs 22 per kg, but the group must pay Rs 3,200 for the stall, transport and a person's time. In Plan 2 the group takes the stall, sells what the market buys at Rs 22 and sells the remainder to the wholesaler at Rs 9. In Plan 3 it sells all 500 kg to the wholesaler.
(a) Name the two links between the farmers and the final consumers, and work out what per cent of the consumer's Rs 25 the farmer gets when he sells to the wholesaler.
(b) Why does the wholesaler need a facility mentioned in the chapter if retailers do not buy at once, and which facility is it?
(c) Work out what the group keeps under Plan 2 if the market buys 200 kg, 250 kg or the full 300 kg, and what it keeps under Plan 3. Which plan is better in each case?
(d) Traders tell the group that the market will take somewhere between 240 kg and 260 kg. Work out Plan 2 at both ends and choose a plan, giving your reason.
questions.a: (a) The wholesaler and the retailer; 9/25 = 36 per cent. (b) Tomatoes are perishable; the chapter says warehouses for perishables may have cold storage facilities at low temperatures, so the wholesaler can hold the stock without loss. (c) Plan 3: 500 x 9 = Rs 4,500. Plan 2 with 200 kg: 200 x 22 - 3,200 + 300 x 9 = 4,400 - 3,200 + 2,700 = Rs 3,900, so Plan 3 is better by Rs 600. With 250 kg: 5,500 - 3,200 + 2,250 = Rs 4,550, so Plan 2 is better by Rs 50. With 300 kg: 6,600 - 3,200 + 1,800 = Rs 5,200, so Plan 2 is better by Rs 700. (d) At 240 kg Plan 2 gives 5,280 - 3,200 + 2,340 = Rs 4,420, which is Rs 80 less than Plan 3; at 260 kg it gives 5,720 - 3,200 + 2,160 = Rs 4,680, Rs 180 more. Plan 2 breaks even with Plan 3 at about 246 kg. Either choice can be defended: Plan 3 risks nothing, Plan 2 risks Rs 80 to gain up to Rs 180 and sells more directly to consumers. A good answer uses both end figures.
s: Part (a): wholesaler and retailer; 36 per cent
Part (b): perishable tomatoes need cold storage in the warehouse
Part (c): Rs 3,900, Rs 4,550 and Rs 5,200 against Rs 4,500, with the better plan in each case
Part (d): Rs 4,420 and Rs 4,680 against Rs 4,500, with a justified choice

questions.q: Hari, a farmer near Nashik, sells tomatoes to a wholesaler at Rs 9 per kg. The wholesaler sells them to a retailer at Rs 18, and the retailer sells to consumers at Rs 25. Hari says, 'The retailer buys at Rs 18, sells at Rs 25 and does nothing for the Rs 7.' (a) Using the chapter, what does the retailer provide to a family that the wholesaler does not? (b) If there were no retailer, what would a family wanting 2 kg of tomatoes have to do?
questions.a: (a) The retailer is the shopkeeper near households who sells in smaller quantities, and the products are meant for consumption; the wholesaler buys and sells in large quantities. The retailer thereby increases the availability of goods to households. (b) It would have to go to the wholesaler or the mandi, where goods are handled in large quantities (an inference); a family wanting 2 kg would find that awkward. Whether Rs 7 is a fair reward is not decided by the chapter.
s: Part (a): small quantities for consumption near households, against the wholesaler's large quantities
Part (b): without a retailer the family faces bulk buying at the wholesaler or mandi (inference)

questions.q:
Match each problem in Column A with what the chapter offers to meet it, in Column B.
Column A: 1. A grape wholesaler fears spoilage while waiting for buyers  2. A wholesaler cannot reach many shops spread over rough terrain  3. A manufacturer wants buyers across the country to find its goods at one place on a phone  4. Families need small quantities of goods close to their homes
Column B: a. a distributor  b. an aggregator  c. a retailer  d. cold storage in the warehouse
questions.a: Perishables need cold storage; distributors bridge the gap created by distances and terrain; an aggregator combines the offers of many sellers at one place online; retailers sell small quantities near households. The wrong pairings swap distributor with aggregator or retailer with aggregator.

questions.q: A builder needs 400 floor tiles, cement and paint for a school extension. (a) The chapter says wholesale markets exist for commodities other than farm produce. Which of the builder's goods does it name, and where would the builder find the bulk supply? (b) Why would the same builder not buy her 400 tiles from a retail store near her home, going by what the chapter says retailers do?
questions.a: (a) The chapter lists construction materials (along with chemicals, electronic items and components, automotive parts) as having wholesale markets, so the builder would look for the wholesale market for construction materials. (b) Retailers sell in smaller quantities to final consumers, and their goods are meant for consumption rather than resale; a builder needing bulk quantities is better served by a wholesaler who buys in large quantities from producers. That a retail store would be costlier or short of stock is an inference.
s: Part (a): construction materials named and the wholesale market as the bulk source
Part (b): retailers sell small quantities to final consumers, so bulk needs go to wholesalers

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Retailers help increase the availability of goods and services to households.
Reason (R): Distances and terrain make it difficult for wholesalers to reach a large number of retailers.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are in the chapter. But R explains why distributors are needed between wholesalers and retailers, not why retailers increase availability of goods to households: that is because retailers are the shops near households selling in small quantities. So R is true but does not explain A.

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'In an online order, the manufacturer sends bulk goods to the aggregator's warehouse, and the aggregator then passes each order to a wholesaler, who delivers it to the buyer.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. The first half is right: manufacturers send bulk quantities to the warehouse of the business that sells through the app, the aggregator. The second half is wrong: the aggregator itself packs the products and delivers them to the online buyer, and the chapter names no wholesaler at that stage.
s: Verdict: agrees only partly
Accepts that bulk goods go from the manufacturer to the aggregator's warehouse
Rejects the wholesaler's delivery: the aggregator packs and delivers

questions.q: Reema runs a small shop. She buys 200 kg of pulses a week from a wholesaler in Pune and sells 1 kg packets to nearby families. Her cousin says, 'You buy 200 kg at once, so you are a wholesaler.' Which reply is correct, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter calls the shopkeepers near households who sell to final consumers retailers; unlike wholesalers they sell in smaller quantities and the products are meant for consumption rather than resale. How much a shop buys does not decide its role: Reema sells 1 kg packets to families. A distributor supplies goods from manufacturers and wholesalers to retailers, and storing stock does not make a shop a wholesaler.
o: No: she is a retailer, a shopkeeper near homes selling small quantities to consumers
Yes: anyone who buys in large quantities from a wholesaler becomes a wholesaler
No: she is a distributor, since she serves families living far from the wholesaler
Yes: she stores the pulses in her shop, just as wholesalers store grains in godowns

questions.q: Compare how goods reach the buyer in a physical market and in an online market. Analyse which links are common and which are different, and say why distributors matter in one of them.
questions.a: Physical: producers or manufacturers, wholesalers (godowns, mandis), distributors, retailers and then consumers. Online: manufacturers send bulk goods to the aggregator's warehouse, and the aggregator packs and delivers to the consumer. Common: producers at the start and the consumer at the end. Different: in the online chain the aggregator handles the stages after the manufacturer, receiving bulk goods, packing and delivering to the doorstep; the chapter does not name a wholesaler or retailer in that chain. Distributors matter in the physical chain because distance and terrain make it hard for wholesalers to reach many retailers; they bridge the gap.
s: Physical chain stages
Online chain stages
Common links
The aggregator and doorstep delivery as the difference
Distributors bridging distance and terrain

questions.q: The chapter says Surat's location on the west coast led to the setting up of ports and road networks that continue to be important today. (a) Name the two facilities, and say which one a Surat exporter sending sarees to a shop in Dubai depends on most. (b) Explain how the other helps a Surat wholesaler who supplies shops across the country.
questions.a: (a) Ports and road networks (the book text names these two; the map in the figure also shows a railway, but the text does not link it to Surat's location). The exporter depends most on the port, since goods must cross the sea to another country; this is an inference. (b) Roads let the wholesaler send fabric to retailers in other states, so he can reach many shops; this is an inference from the chapter's description of the wholesaler's role.
s: Part (a): ports and road networks, with the port chosen for exports
Part (b): a reasoned link between roads and supply across the country

questions.q: A wholesaler tells a customer, 'We sell to the shops near homes and to the final consumers who shop there.' Which statement, based on the chapter, corrects him?
o: Only retailers sell to the final consumers
Wholesalers store the goods they buy in large godowns
Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers
Wholesalers supply goods to the shops near households
questions.a: The chapter says wholesalers buy in large quantities from producers and supply goods to the shops near households, the retailers; the retailers sell to final consumers. The statement 'Only retailers sell to the final consumers' is the chapter's contrast between the wholesaler and the retailer (the word 'only' is the contrast, not a quotation), and it corrects his claim that the wholesaler sells directly to final consumers. The other three statements are true of wholesalers but do not correct him.

questions.q: Take any packaged food item you like. Write a flow of goods from the producer to you in at least four stages, naming the role at each stage.
questions.a: Any valid chain, e.g. wheat farmer (producer) - flour mill (manufacturer) - wholesaler (godown) - distributor - retailer (grocery store) - consumer; each stage correctly named with its role.
s: Four or more stages in a sensible order
Each stage named with the role it plays
Ends with the retailer selling to the consumer

questions.q: True or False? 'A salon can be a retail store even though it sells a service and not goods that a customer carries home.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says retail stores also exist for services like salons, movie theatres and restaurants. Retailers sell to final consumers in smaller quantities, and what makes a seller a retailer is serving final consumers near households, not whether the product is a good or a service.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: retail stores exist for services such as salons; retailers serve final consumers

questions.q:
A grape wholesaler in Nashik stores 20 tonnes (20,000 kg) of grapes worth Rs 60 per kg. Assume that without cold storage 15 per cent of the grapes spoil in 5 days and 5 per cent in 2 days. With cold storage only 3 per cent spoil in either period, but the cold store charges Rs 25,000 per day.
(a) What name does the chapter give to goods such as grapes that spoil quickly, and what facility may a warehouse for them have?
(b) What is the value of the grapes that spoil in 5 days without cold storage, and which link in the chain, the farmer or the wholesaler, bears this loss?
(c) What is the total cost of cold storage for 5 days, counting the rent and the value of the grapes that still spoil?
(d) The buyers from the mandi will collect the grapes in just 2 days. Should the wholesaler use cold storage? Decide, with figures.
questions.a: (a) Perishables; cold storage facilities that keep a low temperature. (b) 15% of 20,000 = 3,000 kg, worth 3,000 x 60 = Rs 1,80,000. The wholesaler bears it, because he has bought the produce from the farm and is holding it in his warehouse. (c) Spoilage 3% = 600 kg = Rs 36,000; rent 5 x 25,000 = Rs 1,25,000; total Rs 1,61,000, which is less than Rs 1,80,000. (d) For 2 days: without cold storage 5% = 1,000 kg = Rs 60,000; with it 36,000 + 2 x 25,000 = Rs 86,000. So for only 2 days cold storage costs more, and the wholesaler need not use it; it pays only when produce must be kept longer.
s: Part (a): perishables; cold storage
Part (b): Rs 1,80,000 and the wholesaler as the link holding the loss
Part (d): no cold storage for 2 days, as Rs 86,000 exceeds Rs 60,000

questions.q: Ravi says, 'A market helps only the sellers. If all the markets in town closed, buyers would lose nothing, because they could make whatever they need at home.' Which statement from the chapter weakens his claim most directly?
o: Markets give access to goods people need but cannot produce themselves
Markets let producers learn what consumers would like to buy in future
Markets can be at a physical place or can be found online as well
Markets connect people, traditions and ideas over many generations
questions.a: Ravi claims buyers could make whatever they need at home. The chapter says markets help individuals, households and businesses access goods and services that they need and cannot produce themselves, which answers him directly. The other three are also in the chapter but address something else: what producers learn from consumers, where markets are, and the non-economic side.

questions.q: For twenty years Rajni's family has had its clothes stitched by the same tailor. (a) Separate what the chapter would call the economic side and the non-economic side of this relationship: she pays Rs 600 for each outfit; he lets her settle the account at the month's end; he is invited to every family wedding. (b) Rajni's brother says, 'The wedding invitations show that a market's main job is friendship.' How does the chapter answer him?
questions.a: (a) Economic: the Rs 600 paid for stitching, an exchange of money for a service. Non-economic: the monthly account and the wedding invitation, which are trusted relationships built across years (the chapter names a monthly account with a grocer as such an example). (b) The chapter says the primary role of the market is to promote economic activities; the relationship is a non-economic significance in addition to that, so friendship is not the main job.
s: Part (a): payment as economic; monthly account and invitation as non-economic
Part (b): economic activity is primary, relationship is an addition

questions.q: A haldi and kumkum seller in Madurai gives every buyer a small pinch of each, free of charge. A classmate says the seller is losing money for nothing. Which reading fits the chapter best?
o: It is a tradition beyond buying and selling, given as good wishes
It is a way to bring in more customers and so more income
It is a price discount that the government has asked sellers to give
It is a quality mark showing that the haldi is safe to eat
questions.a: The chapter describes sellers of haldi and kumkum in south India giving a small quantity of each at no charge as a mark of auspiciousness and good wishes, a practice that goes beyond just buying and selling. The chapter gives good wishes, not more income, as the reason; it is not a government rule or a certification mark.

questions.q: Many families in a town begin asking shopkeepers for millet biscuits instead of maida biscuits. Trace how this demand can pass along the chain of retailers, wholesalers and producers, and say what the producers do. Which example in the chapter works in the same way?
questions.a: Consumers ask retailers for millet biscuits; retailers order more from wholesalers or distributors; the orders reach the producers, who get an indication of what consumers would buy and make more millet biscuits. The chapter's own example is refrigerators that use less electricity, which benefits society.
s: Consumers' request reaches the retailers
It passes back through wholesalers to the producers, who make more of the product
Names the chapter's energy-efficient refrigerator example

questions.q: A Surat cloth maker cannot grow cotton, so she must buy it from the market as an input. For every 10 metres of cloth she needs 2.4 kg of cotton, bought at Rs 100 per kg. When the cotton price rises to Rs 125 per kg, the cost of cotton for each 10 metres rises by Rs ___.

Assertion (A): Ima Keithal provides employment and is an important source of income for thousands of families.
Reason (R): Ima Keithal is a melting pot of cultures, where people from different communities exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both statements are in the chapter. The market gives income because its shops sell vegetables, clothes, handloom and daily essentials to buyers; the mixing of cultures is a separate benefit. R therefore does not explain A.

questions.q:
A town council wants to shift a women's market of 3,000 traders, like Ima Keithal, into a new complex. At present the average trader earns Rs 14,000 a month. In the new complex rents are higher: only 80 per cent of the traders could afford to stay, but those who stay would earn Rs 19,000 a month, because the complex is on a busy road.
