(a) The chapter describes two kinds of significance of a market. Name one benefit of Ima Keithal under each.
(b) Compare the total monthly earning of all traders now and after the move, in crore rupees.
(c) How many traders would lose their place, and which of the benefits in (a) is then most at risk?
(d) Should the council accept the plan? Decide, weighing the figures against what the chapter says such a market gives to people.
questions.a: (a) Economic: employment and income for thousands of families. Non-economic: it is a melting pot of cultures where communities exchange ideas and shared traditions. (b) Now 3,000 x 14,000 = Rs 4.2 crore; after the move 2,400 x 19,000 = Rs 4.56 crore, Rs 36 lakh more. (c) 20% of 3,000 = 600 traders lose their place; the income of their families is most at risk, and the mixing of communities may also be reduced if those who cannot afford the rent belong to particular communities. (d) Either decision can be defended. Accept: total earnings rise by Rs 36 lakh and each trader who stays earns Rs 5,000 more. Reject or change: 600 families lose their only market income and the market's role as a meeting place of communities is damaged. The answer must use the figures and the chapter's two roles, and may propose a middle course such as lower rents.
s: Part (a): an economic and a non-economic benefit named
Part (b): Rs 4.2 crore and Rs 4.56 crore
Part (c): 600 traders; income of their families (and possibly the mixing of communities) at risk
Part (d): a decision weighing the Rs 36 lakh gain against the lost places and the chapter's two roles

questions.q: In one town in a week the numbers are: hand-carved wooden temple models, 2 sellers and 5 buyers; wedding-hall decoration sets, 2 sellers and 300 buyers; handloom sarees, 50 sellers and 5 buyers; school bags, 30 sellers and 700 buyers. Following the chapter's account of Aakriti's paintings, for which product will a seller find it hardest to know where to sell and what price buyers will accept?
o: Hand-carved wooden temple models, with 2 sellers and 5 buyers
Wedding-hall decoration sets, with 2 sellers and 300 buyers in the week
Handloom sarees, with 50 sellers and 5 buyers in the week in town
School bags, with 30 sellers and 700 buyers in the week in town
questions.a: Aakriti's difficulty is that there are few local buyers and sellers of her kind of product, so she has little idea where to sell or what price to ask, unlike the guava seller. The temple models have both few buyers and few sellers. The decoration sets have few sellers but plenty of buyers, and the sarees have few buyers but many sellers, so each has only half the problem (an inference from the chapter's example); school bags have many of both.

questions.q: True or False? 'A family that has stayed with the same tailor for decades is still taking part in the economic role of the market, because it still pays for the stitching, even though the trust between them has grown.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The family still pays the tailor for stitching, which is the economic activity that the chapter calls the primary role of the market. The trust that grew over decades is a non-economic significance in addition to that role; it does not replace it.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: the family still pays for stitching, and the relationship is an addition to the economic role, not a replacement

questions.q: Imagine a town where all markets are closed for a month. Trace the order in which the effects would be felt by farmers, by a cloth producer in a textile city, by a family and by an artist like Aakriti, using ideas from the chapter, and say which effect reaches the family last and why.
questions.a: First, farmers could not sell rice, wheat, dal, vegetables and fruits, so they would earn nothing. Next, a cloth producer could not buy cotton as an input, so production would stop. Aakriti, who already struggles to find buyers, would have no way to sell. The family feels the effects last, as the goods from farmers and cloth producers stop reaching the shops: it could not get what it needs and cannot produce itself, such as food and cloth. Throughout, the town would lose the interactions and traditions that markets carry. The order is traced by inference from the chapter's network.
s: Farmers could not sell, so no income
Cloth producer could not buy cotton as an input, so output stops
The artist has no way to reach buyers
The family is affected last, unable to get goods it cannot produce itself
Loss of interaction and traditions

questions.q: A supermarket opens near Mrs Iyer's house and sells rice at Rs 56 per kg, Rs 2 less than her grocer's Rs 58. Her family buys 25 kg of rice every month and has kept a monthly account with the same grocer for 30 years; it continues to buy from him. Which statement gives both the extra amount she pays in a year and a reading that fits the chapter?
o: She pays Rs 600 more a year, and markets also carry lasting relationships that matter beside price
She pays Rs 50 more a year, and markets also carry lasting trusted relationships that can matter beside price
She pays Rs 600 more a year, and the chapter says buyers should always choose the lowest price offered
She pays Rs 600 more a year, and the grocer has become an aggregator that combines many sellers' offers
questions.a: Extra per kg Rs 2 x 25 kg = Rs 50 a month, and 50 x 12 = Rs 600 a year. The chapter says that, besides the primary economic role, markets have non-economic significance: relationships develop between buyers and sellers across generations, like a family's monthly account with the grocer. It does not say buyers should always take the lowest price, and an aggregator is a website or app combining many sellers' offers. Rs 50 is only the monthly figure.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the role of markets.
1. When many consumers begin to ask for refrigerators that use less electricity, producers get an indication of what consumers would buy.
2. A family's long-lasting trusted relationship with its tailor is a non-economic significance of markets, in addition to their economic role.
3. About 30,000 women own and run all the shops of Ima Keithal in Imphal.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are in the chapter. Statement 3 is false: the chapter says about 3000 women own and run the shops of Ima Keithal.

questions.q:
A fan company sells a standard ceiling fan at Rs 2,200 and an energy-saving fan, which uses less electricity, at Rs 3,400. Its yearly sales are:
Year 1: standard 8,000, energy-saving 2,000.
Year 2: standard 6,000, energy-saving 4,500.
Year 3: standard 3,500, energy-saving 7,500.
(a) Which idea from the chapter does the shift in sales show, and who else gains from it besides the company?
(b) What was the share of energy-saving fans in the sales of Year 1 and of Year 3, in per cent, correct to one decimal place?
(c) Trace how the shift reaches the factory: name in order the three links through which the shoppers' demand would pass, using the chapter's network of participants.
(d) The managers must plan Year 4. Should they stop making the standard fan entirely? Decide, using the price difference and the Year 3 sales.
questions.a: (a) Consumers' choices guide what producers make: buyers are moving to fans that use less electricity, as with the chapter's refrigerators, and society gains from less electricity being used. (b) Year 1: 2,000 / 10,000 = 20.0 per cent; Year 3: 7,500 / 11,000 = 68.2 per cent. (c) Consumers ask the retailers; the retailers' orders pass to wholesalers or distributors; their orders reach the producers, who get an indication of what consumers would buy and make more energy-saving fans. (d) The rising share is the consumers' signal, so the company should make more energy-saving fans. Still, 3,500 buyers chose the standard fan in Year 3, and it costs Rs 1,200 less, so some households may not afford the other; a reasoned plan is to cut but not end it unless the company is sure those buyers will switch.
s: Part (a): consumers' choices guide producers; society gains
Part (b): 20.0 per cent and 68.2 per cent
Part (c): retailers, then wholesalers or distributors, then producers
Part (d): a decision using the price difference and the Year 3 buyers of the standard fan

questions.q: A town divides its market into two walled sections, one for traders of each of two communities, with no common passage. (a) Which role of a market, described through Ima Keithal, is weakened? (b) Does this stop buying and selling? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The role of a melting pot of cultures, where people from different communities come together to exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions. (b) No. Shops can still sell and buyers can still buy, so the economic role continues; what is lost is the mixing, a non-economic significance.
s: Part (a): the melting-pot role, communities meeting and exchanging ideas
Part (b): economic role continues, non-economic mixing is lost

questions.q: A reporter visits Ima Keithal and notes three things. Line 1: a vegetable vendor says her stall has paid her daughter's college fees. Line 2: two vendors from different communities swap festival recipes while closing their stalls. Line 3: a woman from a nearby village buys a handloom shawl that she could not weave herself. Which pairing correctly matches each line with the benefit of a market that the chapter describes?
questions.a: The vendor's fees show the market as a source of employment and income; the swapping of recipes by people of different communities shows the melting pot of cultures, exchanging ideas and shared traditions; the shawl shows markets helping a person access goods she needs or wants and cannot produce herself. The other pairings swap two of these.
o: 1: employment and income; 2: melting pot of cultures; 3: access to goods one cannot produce
1: melting pot of cultures; 2: employment and income; 3: access to goods one cannot produce
1: employment and income; 2: access to goods one cannot produce; 3: melting pot of cultures
1: access to goods one cannot produce; 2: employment and income; 3: melting pot of cultures

questions.q: Neha says, 'The main work of a market is building friendships among people. Buying and selling comes second.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: Not at all. The chapter says the primary role of the market is to promote economic activities, which involve monetary exchange. Relationships, such as with a family tailor or a grocer's monthly account, are a non-economic significance in addition to that role, not a replacement for it.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Cites the primary role as economic activity involving monetary exchange
Treats relationships as an added, non-economic significance, with an example

questions.q: The cotton market of a textile city is shut for a week. (a) What do the cloth producers of the city lose, and what follows for their output? (b) Which later link of the chain feels it next, and how does a family buying a shirt feel it?
questions.a: (a) They lose the input, cotton, which they cannot produce themselves, so they cannot make cloth. (b) Wholesalers and retailers have no cloth to sell, so the family cannot get the shirt cloth, a good it cannot produce itself. The chain is traced by inference from the chapter's description of the network.
s: Part (a): cotton as the input they cannot make, so cloth output stops
Part (b): the next link has no cloth to sell and the family cannot get the shirt

questions.q:
Aakriti paints in oils. At a local fair she can sell about 2 paintings a month at Rs 6,000 each. An app that shows her paintings to buyers in other cities could sell about 8 a month at Rs 5,000 each, but the app takes a 10 per cent commission on each sale, charges a listing fee of Rs 4,000 a month, and she pays Rs 500 for packing and posting each painting. Friends warn that in the first months she may sell only 3.
(a) Why does Aakriti find it hard to sell and price her paintings locally, according to the chapter?
(b) What does she earn a month at the fair, and what does she keep from the app if 8 sell?
(c) What does she keep from the app if only 3 sell, and how many sales a month does she need to match the fair?
(d) How does the chapter's description of an online market explain the larger number of buyers?
(e) Advise her, naming what she cannot be sure of.
questions.a: (a) There are fewer local buyers and sellers of artwork, unlike the case of guavas. (b) Fair: 2 x 6,000 = Rs 12,000. App with 8 sales: 40,000 - 4,000 commission - 4,000 fee - 8 x 500 = 4,000 posting = Rs 28,000. (c) With 3 sales: 15,000 - 1,500 - 4,000 - 1,500 = Rs 8,000, which is Rs 4,000 less than the fair. Each sale adds 5,000 - 500 - 500 = Rs 4,000 after the fee, so she needs (12,000 + 4,000) / 4,000 = 4 sales to match the fair. (d) On an app buyers and sellers need not meet and may be thousands of kilometres apart, so many more buyers can be reached. (e) She cannot be sure that 8 buyers will come each month. A reasoned advice is accepted, for example: keep the fair as the base and try the app, since at 4 or more sales it matches or beats the fair, while at 3 sales it earns Rs 4,000 less.
s: Part (a): few local buyers and sellers
Part (b): Rs 12,000 at the fair and Rs 28,000 from the app at 8 sales
Part (c): Rs 8,000 at 3 sales and 4 sales needed to match the fair
Part (d): online reaches buyers far away who need not meet the seller
Part (e): an uncertainty named and a reasoned advice

questions.q: Describe in about four lines a relationship between your family and a shopkeeper, tailor or doctor. Show one economic side and one non-economic side of it.
questions.a: Any suitable account, e.g. 'We have bought books from Sharma Uncle for ten years. We pay for what we take (economic). He remembers our needs and greets my grandmother (relationship and trust).' It must show both sides.
s: A real or realistic buyer-seller relationship described
Economic side: exchange of goods or services for money
Non-economic side: trust, goodwill or tradition

questions.q: A school's parent body opens a Saturday market where families sell homemade goods, and the head says, 'We only want income for the school fund.' (a) Name two non-economic benefits that the chapter says a market of this kind can bring. (b) Would a purely online version of this market bring the same benefits? Reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: families meet and build relationships and trust that can last across years; people from different communities come together to exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions (as in Ima Keithal). (b) Less so. The chapter says people in a physical market can meet the seller, whereas online buyers and sellers transact from far away without meeting, so the meeting and sharing of traditions is likely to be weaker; this is an inference.
s: Part (a): two non-economic benefits such as relationships and the exchange of ideas and traditions
Part (b): online transacting without meeting weakens them (inference)

questions.q: Which of these shows the government ensuring quality and safety standards, as the chapter describes, and not controlling a price?
o: Approving a new medicine through set procedures and sample testing
Allowing no lifesaving drug to be sold above a fixed upper limit
Announcing that paddy cannot be sold below a set minimum price
Requiring employers to pay workers at least a fixed amount for a day's work
questions.a: The chapter says the government sets procedures for approvals of medicines and conducts sample testing to check that the produced drug meets standards of quality, so there is no risk to consumers' health. The other three are price controls: a maximum price for drugs, a minimum price for paddy and a minimum wage.

questions.q: A factory makes 2 lakh single-use plastic cups a month and earns a profit of Rs 3 on each packet of 10 cups. The cups clog the town's drains, and the town spends Rs 1,50,000 a month to clear them. (a) Compare the factory's monthly profit with the cost borne by the town. (b) Who bears this cost, and what does the chapter say the government does in such a case?
questions.a: (a) 2,00,000 cups make 20,000 packets, so profit = 20,000 x 3 = Rs 60,000; the town's cost is Rs 1,50,000, which is Rs 90,000 more. (b) The townspeople, who are not the cup makers and need not be the buyers, bear it. The chapter says the government plays a crucial role in controlling such effects and intervenes with strict regulations to mitigate the negative effects.
s: Part (a): Rs 60,000 profit against Rs 1,50,000 cost
Part (b): the townspeople bear it; the government regulates

questions.q: Dust from a cement plant makes the families in the nearby village ill. The families never buy the plant's cement, and the cement itself meets every quality standard. Which role of the government in markets, as the chapter describes, applies to this problem?
o: Mitigating the external effects of markets, such as pollution, by regulation
Ensuring quality and safety standards in the cement that the plant makes
Controlling the price of cement to protect buyers and sellers of the cement
Providing a public good that the plant itself does not expect to profit from
questions.a: The chapter says markets sometimes have significant effects beyond the selling and buying, for example pollution from factories, and the government intervenes with strict regulations to mitigate them. Quality standards would apply to the cement itself, which already meets them; a price control does nothing for the villagers' health; and the dust is not a public good the plant supplies.

questions.q:
A new fever tablet is about to be sold. A manufacturer complains that approval procedures and sample testing slow its launch.
(a) What steps does the chapter say the government takes about medicines?
(b) What could go wrong for consumers if there were no sample testing?
(c) How would you reply to the manufacturer?
(d) The chapter also warns about rules. Say what balance the government should keep.
questions.a: (a) It sets procedures for approvals of medicines and conducts sample testing to check whether the produced drug meets standards of quality. (b) A drug that does not meet standards could reach consumers and put their health at risk; the testing is there so that there is no risk to consumers' health. (c) The checks protect the people who take the medicine; a delay is the price of safety, and a tablet that fails does not serve the manufacturer's customers either. (d) The chapter says governments make rules to ensure markets work fairly and consumers are not exploited, but too many rules can make it difficult for markets to function properly. So the checks should be enough to protect health, without piling on needless rules.
s: Part (a): approval procedures and sample testing
Part (b): risk to consumers' health from drugs below standard
Part (c): a reasoned reply to the manufacturer
Part (d): the chapter's warning that too many rules make it difficult for markets to function
Part (d): a balanced conclusion

questions.q: A town spends Rs 6 lakh a year on a free public park and Rs 9 lakh on a ticketed zoo that earns Rs 11 lakh from tickets. Taking the chapter's view of who provides what, the cost per year of the free public good the government provides, shared over the town's 30,000 residents, is Rs ___ per resident.

Read the statements about the government's role.
1. A minimum price for paddy is set to protect consumers from being overcharged.
2. Minimum wages are set so that employees make fair payments to employers.
3. Kautilya's Arthashastra told ghee traders to give buyers 1/50 part more to make up for the ghee sticking to the measuring can.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Only statement 3 is from the chapter. Statement 1 reverses the purpose: a minimum price for crops protects farmers from losses. Statement 2 reverses the payers: minimum wages ensure that employers make fair payments to employees.

questions.q: Meera says, 'Producers sell goods to make a profit. Parks, roads and policing are goods on which they expect only a small profit, so the government provides them.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. The first sentence is right: the chapter says producers make and sell goods and services to be able to make a profit. But the chapter says that on public parks, roads and policing producers do not expect to make a profit at all, not a small one. Because of that, the government provides these public goods and services for the society.
s: Verdict: agrees only partly
Accepts that producers sell to make a profit
Corrects 'a small profit': producers expect no profit on parks, roads and policing, so the government provides them

questions.q: A state announces that onions cannot be sold above Rs 30 per kg. Onion traders, whose cost is Rs 34 per kg, say they will stop bringing onions to the town markets. Which idea from the chapter does the traders' reaction illustrate?
questions.a: The chapter says that if the price is too low, producers would not have any motivation to produce. A limit of Rs 30 against a cost of Rs 34 means a loss on every kilogram, so the traders stay away. The other ideas are in the chapter but do not describe this case: no consumer is being charged too much, the issue is one limit rather than a pile of rules, and onions are not a public good.
o: If the price limit is too low, producers have no motivation to produce
If prices are too high, consumers are disadvantaged by what they must pay
Too many rules can make it difficult for markets to function properly
Producers do not expect to make a profit on goods the government supplies

questions.q:
A weights-and-measures inspector weighs five packets marked '1 kg sugar' from each of three shops (in grams).
Shop A: 1000, 995, 1005, 1000, 1000.
Shop B: 980, 975, 990, 985, 970.
Shop C: 940, 950, 945, 955, 960.
Sugar sells at Rs 48 per kg. Shop C sells about 200 such packets a day and Shop B about 1,500. Shop C was warned twice earlier this year about short packets; Shop B has never been warned.
(a) Which government role from the chapter is the inspector carrying out?
(b) By how many grams, on average, is a packet from Shop C below the label?
(c) What is the value of the sugar that customers fail to receive in a day, at Shop C and at Shop B?
(d) The inspector has time for a full check of only one shop this week. Which should she choose, and what should be done about the other two, keeping in mind the chapter's warning about too many rules?
questions.a: (a) Monitoring the weights and measures of packaged products, to check the net quantity in the package. (b) 940 + 950 + 945 + 955 + 960 = 4,750 g, so 250 g short over five packets, 50 g per packet. (c) Shop C: 200 x 50 g = 10 kg, worth 10 x 48 = Rs 480 a day. Shop B: the five packets total 4,900 g, 20 g short on average; 1,500 x 20 g = 30 kg, worth 30 x 48 = Rs 1,440 a day. (d) Either choice can be defended. Shop B: its customers lose three times as much sugar a day. Shop C: its packets are far shorter each time (50 g against 20 g) and it has been warned twice, so repeated short packing is the bigger offence. Whichever she picks, the other should get a milder, graded response such as a warning or a re-check later, Shop A needs no action, and the response should not be excessive, since too many rules can make it difficult for markets to function.
s: Part (a): monitoring weights and measures
Part (b): 50 g per packet
Part (c): Rs 480 a day at C and Rs 1,440 a day at B
Part (d): a choice backed by the daily loss, with graded action and the warning about too many rules

questions.q: True or False? 'Every cup from the single-use plastic cup factory is bought by a willing buyer, so the town has no business making rules about the factory.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says markets sometimes have significant effects beyond the selling and buying, such as pollution from factories making single-use plastics, which poses health risks. The government intervenes with strict regulations to mitigate them, so the buyers' willingness does not settle the matter.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: markets can affect people who are not buyers or sellers, such as through pollution, which the government regulates

questions.q: (a) Explain why the government sets an upper limit on the price of lifesaving drugs but a lower limit on the price of paddy. (b) What does the chapter say can go wrong if the limit is set badly in each case?
questions.a: (a) Buyers of lifesaving drugs need them and could be overcharged, so the limit caps what the seller can charge; farmers who grow paddy could face losses if the price fell too low, so the limit sets the least they can be paid. (b) If a price limit is too low, producers would not have any motivation to produce (a risk for drugs capped too low); if prices are too high, consumers would be disadvantaged (a risk for a paddy floor set too high). The pairing of each risk with its product is an inference.
s: Part (a): upper limit protects buyers from overcharging, lower limit protects farmers from losses
Part (b): too low, no motivation to produce; too high, consumers disadvantaged

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Public parks, roads and policing are provided by the government.
Reason (R): Governments make rules to ensure markets work fairly and consumers are not exploited.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are in the chapter, but R does not explain A. The chapter says the government provides parks, roads and policing because they are goods and services on which producers do not expect to make a profit; making fair rules is a different role of the government.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: An inspector weighs 8 packets of rice, each marked 500 g, and finds that together they weigh 3.76 kg. Show that all eight packets cannot hold what the label says, and name the government role being used.
questions.a: 8 x 500 g = 4,000 g = 4 kg, but the packets weigh only 3.76 kg, which is 240 g less. So they cannot all be full. The government checks the weights and measures of packaged goods to see the net quantity in the package.
s: Computes 4 kg expected
Shows the shortfall of 240 g
Names monitoring weights and measures as the role

questions.q: A town wants its street food to be safe. It already requires one licence and sample testing of food. It now adds eleven further permits, each from a different office and each taking weeks. Which assessment best fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says governments make rules so that markets work fairly and consumers are not exploited, but too many rules can make it difficult for markets to function properly. A licence and sample testing fit the first part; eleven more permits fit the warning. The chapter does not say more rules always protect further, nor that markets alone assure safety, and permits are not public goods.
o: The first checks protect consumers, but the added permits risk hampering markets
Every extra permit protects consumers further, as the chapter says more rules mean fairer markets
None of the checks is needed, since the chapter says markets alone keep food safe for consumers
The permits are public goods, since the government provides them and producers do not profit

questions.q: A state law says a contractor must pay each labourer at least Rs 450 a day; the contractor has been paying Rs 400. He employs 40 labourers for 26 days in a month. (a) How much more does the law add to his monthly wage bill? (b) Whom does the chapter say a minimum wage protects, and in what way?
questions.a: (a) The rise is Rs 50 a day, so 40 x 26 x 50 = Rs 52,000 a month. (b) The employees: the government sets minimum wages for work done so that employers make fair payments to them.
s: Part (a): Rs 52,000 a month
Part (b): employees are protected, since employers must make fair payments

questions.q:
A lifesaving tablet costs the maker Rs 380 per strip to make, and the maker produces 10,000 strips a month. The government has set a maximum price of Rs 500 per strip, and each of the 10,000 patients buys one strip a month. The maker warns that its cost will rise to Rs 430 per strip next year. Patients' groups say many patients earn little. Three limits are proposed: Rs 420, Rs 470 and Rs 500.
(a) What is the maker's monthly profit at each limit at today's cost of Rs 380?
(b) What is the maker's monthly result at each limit when the cost is Rs 430, and what does the chapter say about producers when a price limit is set too low?
(c) How much more do the 10,000 patients together pay each month at Rs 500 than at Rs 420, and at Rs 470 than at Rs 420?
(d) Advise the government on one limit, using the chapter's warning about limits that are too low or too high.
questions.a: (a) At Rs 380 cost: Rs 420 gives 40 x 10,000 = Rs 4,00,000; Rs 470 gives 90 x 10,000 = Rs 9,00,000; Rs 500 gives 120 x 10,000 = Rs 12,00,000. (b) At Rs 430 cost: Rs 420 gives a loss of Rs 1,00,000; Rs 470 gives a profit of Rs 4,00,000; Rs 500 gives Rs 7,00,000. The chapter says that if the price is too low, producers would not have any motivation to produce. (c) Rs 500 against Rs 420: 80 x 10,000 = Rs 8,00,000 more; Rs 470 against Rs 420: 50 x 10,000 = Rs 5,00,000 more. (d) Rs 420 would put the maker at a loss once its cost rises, so the drug may stop being made; Rs 500 leaves patients paying the most. Any reasoned choice is accepted: Rs 470 keeps the maker profitable even at the higher cost while costing patients Rs 30 per strip less than Rs 500; Rs 500 may be argued if the maker's supply must be secure; Rs 420 only with a plan to support the maker.
s: Part (b): the results at cost Rs 430, and no motivation to produce when the limit is too low
Part (c): the extra paid by patients at each limit
Part (d): a limit chosen and justified using the figures and the chapter's warning

questions.q: A town council can fund only a public good, which the chapter's glossary describes as a service or commodity accessible to all members of a society, whose present use does not diminish its availability for future use. Which of these qualifies?
questions.a: The footpath is open to every resident, nobody sells it for profit, and one person's walk leaves it as available tomorrow. The borewell is open to all, but its present use does diminish what is left for later, so it fails the glossary's second condition. The amusement park and the bus are run by producers for a profit.
o: A footpath by the river that any resident may use
A free-to-all borewell whose water is almost used up each day
A ticketed amusement park built by a company for profit
A private bus service that charges a fare from each traveller

questions.q: Describe a situation in which the government would need to step in to deal with a harm caused by a market. Name the product, the harm and one step the government could take.
questions.a: Any suitable case, e.g. a factory making single-use plastic bags pollutes drains and harms health; the government could bring in strict rules limiting or banning production.
s: A product or market named
The harm to the environment or health
A government step such as a regulation

questions.q:
Sunita grows 4,000 kg of wheat at a cost of Rs 22 per kg. The government's minimum price for wheat is Rs 24 per kg. In a bumper year without such protection the market price would have fallen to Rs 19 per kg. A proposal is made to raise the minimum price to Rs 30 per kg; assume the market price moves with the minimum price, so consumers pay the extra amount. A family of four uses about 20 kg of wheat a month. Her town has 400 wheat farmers like Sunita, each selling 4,000 kg, and 8,000 families like the one described.
(a) Under which government role in the chapter does a minimum price for wheat come, and whom does it protect?
(b) What would Sunita's loss have been at Rs 19, and what is her profit at Rs 24?
(c) At Rs 30 instead of Rs 24, how much more would each family pay in a year, how much more would all 8,000 families pay, and how much more would all 400 farmers receive?
(d) Should the government raise the minimum price to Rs 30? Decide, using the figures and the chapter's caution about price limits.
questions.a: (a) Controlling prices to protect buyers and sellers; the minimum price protects farmers so that they do not incur losses. (b) At Rs 19: 4,000 x 3 = Rs 12,000 loss. At Rs 24: 4,000 x 2 = Rs 8,000 profit. (c) Each family: 20 x 6 x 12 = Rs 1,440 a year. All 8,000 families: Rs 1,15,20,000. Each farmer gains 4,000 x 6 = Rs 24,000, so 400 farmers gain Rs 96,00,000. (d) Either side can be argued. For: farmers' profit rises from Rs 8,000 to Rs 32,000 and is safer against higher costs. Against: the Rs 24 price already prevents a loss, which is the purpose of the limit; raising it takes Rs 1.152 crore from consumers to give Rs 96 lakh to farmers, and the chapter warns that if prices are too high, consumers are disadvantaged. The answer must use the figures.
s: Part (a): price control; farmers protected
Part (b): loss of Rs 12,000 and profit of Rs 8,000
Part (c): Rs 1,440 per family, Rs 1,15,20,000 for all families and Rs 96,00,000 for all farmers
Part (d): a decision weighing the two totals and the chapter's caution

questions.q: Assume that, in the time of Kautilya's Arthashastra, 1/50 of the ghee in a measure stuck to the measuring can. A trader measures out 2,000 ml for a buyer. (a) How much ghee sticks, and how much extra does the rule require him to give? (b) Which role of the government today, described in the chapter, is closest to this old rule, and what is the difference?
questions.a: (a) 2,000 x 1/50 = 40 ml sticks, so the rule requires him to give 40 ml extra, as manasrava, to compensate for the reduction in quantity owing to the ghee sticking to the measuring can. (b) Monitoring weights and measures of packaged products, which checks the net quantity in the package. Both protect consumers from getting less than they pay for. The difference (an inference): the old rule told the trader to add a fixed extra, while today the government sets up systems to check the quantity in the package.
s: Part (a): 40 ml sticks and 40 ml extra is required, to compensate for the sticking
Part (b): monitoring weights and measures is the closest modern role, with the difference noted

questions.q:
Read the statements about judging quality.
1. A TV with more BEE stars uses less electricity, so the buyer's electricity bill is lower.
2. A buyer should expect to find the BEE Star rating on a bag of cement.
3. A shopper who buys a brand because friends recommend it is using the reputation of the product, built through word of mouth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: BEE stars appear on items such as TVs, laptops and air conditioners; cement is a construction material, for which the chapter names the ISI mark.

questions.q: Dev picks up a packet of instant noodles. The label shows ingredients, MRP and a best before date, but no FSSAI mark. Which response fits the chapter best?
o: Look for other evidence; the FSSAI mark shows government testing
Rely on the ingredients list and best before date, which show it was tested
Look for AGMARK, which the chapter gives for packaged processed foods
Look for the ISI mark, which the chapter names for food items
questions.a: The chapter says the FSSAI mark indicates that food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume; an ingredients list and a best before date do not show testing. AGMARK is the chapter's mark for agricultural products such as vegetables, pulses and honey, not for packaged noodles, and ISI is named for appliances, construction materials, tyres and paper.

questions.q: A shopper says, 'This air conditioner has 5 BEE stars, so it must be the safest and best-made one in the shop.' (a) What do BEE stars tell a buyer, and what do they not tell? (b) Two air conditioners both have 5 stars, but only one carries the ISI mark. Which is the safer bet on quality and safe use, going by the chapter?
questions.a: (a) BEE stars show the energy efficiency of the appliance: higher stars mean it uses less energy and electricity. They do not show how safe or well made it is. (b) The one with the ISI mark, issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards, which ensures quality and that the product is safe to use; the stars on both are equal and say nothing on this.
s: Part (a): stars show energy efficiency, not safety or build
Part (b): the ISI-marked set, since ISI ensures quality and safe use

questions.q:
Match each shopper's situation in Column A with the mark in Column B that the chapter would have the shopper look for.
Column A: 1. A stationery shop checks a ream of paper  2. A buyer wants unprocessed pulses of tested grade  3. A school wants a laptop that costs less to run  4. A family buys a packed snack and wants it tested and safe to eat
Column B: a. ISI mark  b. BEE Star rating  c. FSSAI logo  d. AGMARK
questions.a: The chapter lists paper among the items bearing the ISI mark, AGMARK is the mark for agricultural products such as pulses, BEE stars show how little electricity a laptop uses, and the FSSAI logo shows food has been tested and is safe. The wrong pairings swap AGMARK with ISI or FSSAI, or BEE with FSSAI.

questions.q:
A school kitchen wants 20 jars of honey of 500 g each. Three online sellers offer:
Seller X: Rs 300 a jar, shows FSSAI and AGMARK marks, rating 4.1 stars from 850 reviews.
Seller Y: Rs 240 a jar, shows no certification mark, rating 4.8 stars from 9 reviews.
Seller Z: Rs 280 a jar, shows the FSSAI mark only, rating 4.4 stars from 40 reviews.
(a) Whose rating is the least dependable, and why?
(b) Compare Z with X: what extra does X's AGMARK tell a buyer of honey?
(c) How much more would the school pay for 20 jars from X than from Y, and than from Z?
(d) Which seller would you choose for the school kitchen? Decide, giving one point from marks and one from reviews.
questions.a: (a) Seller Y's (this is reasoning, not a statement in the book): the 4.8 stars come from only 9 reviews, and the product shows no certification mark, so there is little to confirm the rating. (b) AGMARK is the certification mark for agricultural products such as honey, so it adds a second confirmation of quality beyond FSSAI's sign that the food has been tested and is safe. (c) X: 20 x 300 = Rs 6,000; Y: 20 x 240 = Rs 4,800, so Rs 1,200 more; Z: 20 x 280 = Rs 5,600, so Rs 400 more. (d) A defensible choice is X: it has both marks and the most reviews, so its rating is more dependable, and food safety matters in a kitchen. Z is acceptable if argued on its lower price with the FSSAI mark. Y is the cheapest but the least supported.
s: Part (a): Y's rating, with only 9 reviews and no mark
Part (b): AGMARK as the mark for agricultural products such as honey
Part (c): Rs 1,200 and Rs 400
Part (d): a choice with one point from marks and one from reviews

questions.q: A school has 6 air conditioners to buy. A BEE 5-star model uses 400 units a year less than a 3-star model of the same size, and a unit of electricity costs Rs 7. By choosing the 5-star model for all six, the school saves Rs ___ a year on electricity.

A shopper who is allergic to nuts picks up a 1 kg packet of gram flour that carries the FSSAI logo. She has already read the ingredients list, which says only 'gram flour, edible oil', and she thinks, 'Tested and safe, so it is safe for me.' What she still wants to know is whether nuts are handled where it is made. Which label detail is meant to answer that doubt?
o: The allergen declaration
The ingredients list, read again more slowly
The FSSAI logo, since it shows testing
The batch number
questions.a: The FSSAI logo shows that the food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume in general, but that is not a statement about one person's allergy. The ingredients list is what she has already read, and it names what the flour is made of, not what else is handled where it is made. The batch number only traces the lot. The allergen declaration, one of the details listed in the chapter, is the part meant to warn an allergic buyer.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'Buy this 5-star TV instead of the 3-star one and you will save Rs 3,000 on electricity every year.' The 3-star TV uses 250 units a year, the 5-star TV uses 150 units a year, and a unit costs Rs 8. Show that his claim cannot be correct. What does the chapter say a higher star rating does to the bill?
questions.a: 3-star bill: 250 x 8 = Rs 2,000. 5-star bill: 150 x 8 = Rs 1,200. The yearly saving is only Rs 800, so Rs 3,000 is impossible. The chapter says more stars mean the appliance uses less electricity, so the bill is smaller, but not by the amount he says.
s: Both yearly bills worked out
Saving of Rs 800 shown to be less than Rs 3,000
Higher stars mean less electricity and a lower bill

questions.q: A school buys an LED television. The box carries a BEE Star rating of 4 stars and an ISI mark. Which statement fits the chapter?
o: Stars show energy use; the ISI mark shows quality and safe use
Both marks tell how little electricity the television would use
Stars show food-safety testing; the ISI mark shows energy use
The two marks cannot both appear on one product at the same time
questions.a: The chapter says BEE stars on electronic items such as TVs show energy efficiency (more stars, less electricity), while the ISI mark, issued by BIS, is generally present on electrical appliances and ensures quality and that the product is safe to use. Food safety belongs to FSSAI, and nothing in the chapter stops two marks appearing together.

questions.q: True or False? 'A phone cover with hundreds of 5-star online reviews has been tested by a government agency, so it needs no certification mark.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Online reviews and feedback are opinions of other consumers that help a buyer decide whether to buy; they are not a test by a government agency. Certification marks are provided by government agencies and confirm that a product fulfils minimum quality standards.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: reviews come from other consumers, while certification marks come from government agencies

questions.q:
Your parent asks you to buy a 1 kg packet of gram flour. Two packets are on the shelf.
Packet P: net quantity 1 kg, MRP Rs 110, FSSAI logo and licence number, no allergen declaration printed.
Packet Q: net quantity 900 g, MRP Rs 95, no FSSAI logo, allergen declaration 'contains mustard'.
(a) Which packet is the size that was asked for, and by how much is the other short?
(b) Work out the price per 100 g of each packet, correct to two decimal places.
(c) Which label detail shows that Packet P has been tested by the government, and what does this mean for Packet Q?
(d) Your sister is allergic to mustard. Which packet's label can warn her, and what does it say?
(e) The rest of the family has no allergy. Decide which packet to buy for them, giving two reasons from the labels.
questions.a: (a) Packet P is 1 kg; Packet Q holds 900 g, which is 100 g short. (b) P: 110 / 10 = Rs 11.00 per 100 g; Q: 95 / 9 = Rs 10.56 per 100 g (Q is cheaper per 100 g by about 44 paise). (c) The FSSAI logo and licence number: the symbol indicates that the food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume. Packet Q does not show it, so the label gives no sign of that testing. (d) Packet Q, whose allergen declaration says it contains mustard; Packet P prints no allergen declaration, so its label gives her no warning either way. (e) A reasoned decision is accepted. For P: it is the size asked for and carries the FSSAI logo. For Q: it is cheaper per 100 g and warns of the allergen, but it lacks the FSSAI logo and is 100 g short, so many would choose P; Q can be defended on price if the family accepts the shortfall and the missing logo.
s: Part (a): P is 1 kg; Q is 100 g short
Part (b): Rs 11.00 and Rs 10.56 per 100 g
Part (c): FSSAI logo and licence number on P; none on Q
Part (d): Q's allergen declaration warns her; P's label has none
Part (e): a decision with two reasons from the labels

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An air conditioner with more BEE stars is likely to give a lower electricity bill.
Reason (R): BEE stars show how safe the appliance is to touch and use.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: higher stars indicate that the appliance uses less energy and electricity, so the bill is smaller. R is false: BEE stars indicate energy efficiency; safety and quality of an electrical appliance are shown by the ISI mark.

questions.q: A neighbour praises a brand of pressure cooker, and its page on a shopping app shows 4.7 stars from only 6 reviews. (a) Which two sources of quality information other than certification marks is Mira using? (b) Why might she hesitate to depend on either alone?
questions.a: (a) Word of mouth (the neighbour's recommendation, which builds the product's reputation) and online reviews and feedback from other consumers. (b) Both are opinions of other buyers and are not tested by a government agency; six reviews are also very few, so she may look for a certification mark. Accept any reasoned hesitation.
s: Part (a): word of mouth and online reviews
Part (b): a reasoned limit, such as opinions only or very few reviews

questions.q: A school wants a new television. Its first concern is that the set is of good quality and safe to use, and the school pays the electricity bill. Four sets are offered: a three-star set with the ISI mark; a five-star set with the ISI mark; a five-star set with no ISI mark; and a set with 4.8 stars from online reviews and no mark. Going by the chapter, which should it prefer?
questions.a: The ISI mark ensures quality and that the product is safe to use, and more BEE stars mean less electricity, so with both concerns the five-star set with the ISI mark is best. The three-star set has the mark but a higher bill. The five-star set without the mark gives no sign of quality and safety, and online reviews are only the opinions of other consumers.
o: The five-star set with the ISI mark
The three-star set with the ISI mark
The five-star set with no ISI mark
The set with 4.8 stars from online reviews

questions.q: A notice board in your colony needs a shopping tip headed 'Look for the mark'. Write three lines, one each for a packet of pulses, a refrigerator and a car tyre, naming any one suitable mark a buyer should look for and what it tells the buyer.
questions.a: Any suitable tip, e.g. pulses: look for AGMARK, the certification mark for agricultural products (FSSAI shows food tested and safe); refrigerator: look for the BEE Star rating, since more stars mean less electricity (an ISI mark is also found on electrical appliances); car tyre: look for the ISI mark issued by BIS, which ensures quality and safe use. Each line must name a correct mark and what it tells the buyer.
s: Pulses with AGMARK or FSSAI and what it tells
Refrigerator with BEE Star rating or ISI and what it tells
Car tyre with the ISI mark and what it tells

questions.q:
The Menon family wants a new air conditioner and has two choices. A 3-star model costs Rs 38,000 and uses 1,500 units of electricity a year. A 5-star model costs Rs 46,000 and uses 1,000 units a year. A unit costs Rs 8. The family expects to live in the house for 5 years, but it has only Rs 40,000 in savings.
(a) Which label on the air conditioner tells the family which model uses less electricity, and which model does it favour?
(b) What is the yearly electricity bill for each model, and in how many years does the 5-star model recover its extra price?
(c) Besides the family's bill, what benefit does the chapter say lower electricity use brings?
(d) Which model should the family buy? Decide, using the total cost over 5 years, the savings limit and the chapter's point.
questions.a: (a) The BEE Star rating; it favours the 5-star model, since more stars mean less electricity. (b) 1,500 x 8 = Rs 12,000 and 1,000 x 8 = Rs 8,000; the extra price Rs 8,000 is recovered in 8,000 / 4,000 = 2 years. (c) It is good for the environment. questions.q: A website lists two electric kettles. Kettle A shows an ISI mark and has no reviews yet. Kettle B shows no mark and has 4.8 stars from 12 reviews. (a) From whom does each kettle's quality evidence come? (b) Which would you buy for a family with young children, and why?
questions.a: (a) Kettle A: the ISI mark, issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards, a government agency. Kettle B: other consumers, through online reviews and feedback. (b) A reasoned choice: Kettle A, since the mark ensures quality and that the product is safe to use, whereas 12 reviews are few and are only opinions. Kettle B can be chosen only with the reasons that its reviews are more and consistent; the answer must use both kinds of evidence.
s: Part (a): ISI from a government agency, reviews from consumers
Part (b): a reasoned choice using both kinds of evidence

questions.q: Kabir says, 'A BEE Star rating on a laptop shows that the government has tested it and found it safe, in the same way as the FSSAI logo does for food.' Do you agree fully, partly or not at all? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Not at all. The chapter says the FSSAI logo indicates that food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume. BEE stands for Bureau of Energy Efficiency and its stars show how much electricity the product uses; higher stars mean less energy. The star rating is about energy efficiency, not a safety test.
s: Verdict: disagrees
States what FSSAI shows: food tested and safe
States that BEE stars show energy efficiency, not safety

questions.q: Compare certification marks with online reviews and word of mouth as ways of judging quality. Analyse the strengths of each and say which a consumer should depend on when buying medicine or food for the family.
questions.a: Certification marks like FSSAI, ISI and AGMARK are given by government agencies and confirm that a product meets minimum quality standards, so they are dependable for safety. Online reviews and word of mouth come from other buyers and build a product's reputation, helping a buyer decide whether to buy, but they are opinions and are not tested by an agency. For food and medicine, where health is involved, the family should rely first on the certification marks and then use reviews and word of mouth as support. The point that reviews are only opinions is reasoning, not a statement in the chapter.
s: Certification marks given by government agencies
They confirm minimum quality standards
Reviews and word of mouth shape reputation
Difference in reliability
A reasoned choice for food or medicine

questions.q: Before the marbles competition, Rohan has Rs 150 to spend. The chapter lists price, size, strength and attractive colours as things he would look for. (a) Which of these can he check himself, just by looking and handling the marbles in the shop? (b) For a packet of gram flour, why can he not judge quality the same way, and what does the chapter say helps him?
questions.a: (a) Size and attractive colours can be seen, and the price is on the label; strength can be tested by handling or tapping (any two or three of these are accepted). (b) The quality of food, such as whether it is safe and meets the minimum standards, cannot be seen from the packet. The chapter says certification marks given by government agencies, such as the FSSAI logo, confirm that the product fulfils the minimum quality standards; reviews and word of mouth also help.
s: Part (a): qualities that can be checked by looking or handling
Part (b): food quality cannot be seen; certification marks such as FSSAI help
